review.summary: This work introduces a dataset and framework for evaluating semantic parsers’ handling of ambiguity. The dataset contains natural language utterances that are ambiguous in one of four ways (PP attachment, quantifier scope, pronominal coreference, and conjunction), paired with two possible parses. The authors construct two evaluation settings: zero-shot, in which the model is provided with the “ingredients” for both parses but no examples of this ambiguity type, and few-shot, in which the model is shown examples of this ambiguity type with conflicting parses. The authors evaluate LMs on this task and find that they are generally unable to capture both possible parses in the zero-shot setting, but are better at representing the distribution of parses given in the prompt in the few-shot setting.

weaknesses.issue:
- My main concern is that it’s not clear what the takeaway from this work is. In the zero-shot setting, the models are clearly failing to predict both parses. In the few-shot setting, they seem to be doing better, but it’s not clear to me exactly what the target we’re aiming for is. Is the idea that we want models to represent the exact same distribution as the prompt? In that case, I’m not sure why the few-shot setting is better than the zero-shot setting. In the zero-shot setting, the models are given the individual pieces and can thus reason compositionally, whereas in the few-shot setting the models are given a distribution over complete examples, but lack the ability to reason compositionally. A more interesting and useful evaluation setting would be one in which the model is given some examples of this ambiguity type (but not necessarily the specific examples it sees in the prompt), and then tested on its ability to represent the distribution of parses for an unseen sentence. This would evaluate the model’s ability to generalize to new instances of this ambiguity type, which seems like the ultimate goal. 
- The dataset is quite synthetic. The utterances are constructed from templates, and the logical forms (LFs) are quite simple. In general, I’m skeptical that this is a good proxy for how ambiguity is encountered in the real world. In particular, I’m not convinced that the specific utterances in the dataset are actually ambiguous. While the authors show that human annotators disagree on interpretations of these utterances, this doesn’t necessarily mean that both interpretations are “valid” or that the utterance is truly ambiguous. (It could be that one interpretation is more “preferred” or “more likely” and the other is not, for example.) I would have liked to see some more psycholinguistic experiments with humans to verify that these utterances are truly ambiguous (e.g., in a sentence completion task, have subjects complete the sentence in as many different ways as possible and see how many different interpretations they produce, or ask subjects which interpretation they prefer and how confident they are in their choice). As it is, I’m not convinced that the utterances in the dataset are truly ambiguous in the way that the paper claims.
- The analysis of the effect of prompt length in the few-shot setting is interesting, but I’m not sure what to take away from it. It seems like the length of the prompt doesn’t matter much (which is interesting), but then the question is why not just use a very short prompt (i.e., just provide the individual examples and don’t provide any context sentences)? This would be more similar to the zero-shot setting.

3

4

## Contribution
3

The zero-shot setting is a nice way to test the ability to generalize to novel combinations of known components, while the few-shot setting is a better approximation of what we want for real-world performance (i.e., representing the distribution of possible parses given the prompt).
- The analyses are interesting and insightful. The per-token probability heatmap for zero-shot experiments, in particular, reveals interesting differences between the different types of ambiguity.

## Weaknesses
- My main concern is that it’s not clear what the takeaway from this work is. In the zero-shot setting, the models are clearly failing to predict both parses. In the few-shot setting, they seem to be doing better, but it’s not clear to me exactly what the target we’re aiming for is. Is the idea that we want models to represent the exact same distribution as the prompt? In that case, I’m not sure why the few-shot setting is better than the zero-shot setting. In the zero-shot setting, the models are given the individual pieces and can thus reason compositionally, whereas in the few-shot setting the models are given a distribution over complete examples, but lack the ability to reason compositionally. A more interesting and useful evaluation setting would be one in which the model is given some examples of this ambiguity type (but not necessarily the specific examples it sees in the prompt), and then tested on its ability to represent the distribution of parses for an unseen sentence. While the authors show that human annotators disagree on interpretations of these utterances, this doesn’t necessarily mean that both interpretations are “valid” or that the utterance is truly ambiguous. (It could be that one interpretation is more “preferred” or “more likely” and the other is not, for example.) I would have liked to see some more psycholinguistic experiments with humans to verify that these utterances are truly ambiguous (e.g., in a sentence completion task, have subjects complete the sentence in as many different ways as possible and see how many different interpretations they produce, or ask subjects which interpretation they prefer and how confident they are in their choice). review.summary: This paper introduces a new benchmark, AmP, for evaluating models’ ability to parse ambiguous sentences. In contrast to other benchmarks, AmP explicitly includes multiple possible parses for sentences, rather than assuming that there is a single, correct parse. The benchmark consists of sentences with five types of syntactic and semantic ambiguities (e.g., prepositional phrase attachment, scope of quantifiers, etc.). For each ambiguity type, the benchmark provides sentences paired with two different logical forms. The authors evaluate several large pre-trained models in both a zero-shot setting (where the model is prompted with the “components” of the ambiguity, e.g., the individual sentences that make up a prepositional phrase attachment ambiguity) and a few-shot setting (where the model is prompted with examples of the ambiguity type). The authors introduce two metrics for measuring models’ ability to capture ambiguity, a dataset-level metric and an instance-level metric. The results show that models are very bad at recovering both possible parses for sentences in the zero-shot setting. They are somewhat better in the few-shot setting, particularly once the prompts contain more examples of the ambiguity type. The model that comes closest to recovering both possible parses is GPT 3.5 (but only for PP attachment and scope ambiguities). The authors also find that the model’s token-level confidence scores sometimes reflects the alternative parse, particularly for scope, inverse scope, and conjunctions. Human annotations show that the sentences in the dataset are indeed ambiguous (there is a near 50/50 split between the two possible parses). Finally, the authors find that models are relatively good at recovering the distribution of ambiguous parses given in the prompt.

weaknesses.issue:
- The paper focuses exclusively on a few types of syntactic and semantic ambiguities. While these are classic examples of ambiguities, there are many other types of ambiguities, including lexical, discourse, and cultural ambiguities. The authors briefly mention this in the discussion and future work, but it would be nice to see the dataset expanded to include other types of ambiguities.

- The paper focuses exclusively on a few different models, all of which are similar in size and from the CodeGen family. It would be nice to see a wider range of models tested, including smaller and larger models, as well as models from different families. This would help us understand whether there are certain characteristics of models that are particularly relevant for handling ambiguity.

In particular, it is not clear to me why the proposed method needs to be iterative. It would be nice if the authors could explain why the proposed method needs to be iterative and what happens if it is not iterative. 
- The proposed method has many similarities with diffusion models. In particular, it is not clear how the proposed method is different from a diffusion model with a different prior and a different likelihood. # Review

## Summary
This paper proposes a method called LatentDiffuser, which learns a latent action space and a conditional generative model over trajectories in the latent action space. The authors show that under certain conditions, planning in the latent action space is equivalent to energy guided diffusion sampling. The authors perform experiments on low-dimensional locomotion tasks, Adroit, and AntMaze.

## Soundness
2

## Presentation
2

## Contribution
2

## Strengths
The experiments seem thorough, with comparison to many baselines. The proposed method also seems to perform well in these experiments.

## Weaknesses
The writing of this paper is quite poor, making it difficult to understand the technical details. The main contributions are also somewhat unclear.

## Questions
What is the main contribution of this paper? It seems like the main contribution is showing the equivalence between planning in the latent action space and energy guided diffusion sampling. However, this seems to be a relatively minor contribution. Furthermore, the equivalence between planning and diffusion sampling has been explored in prior work [1]. The latent action space learning also seems to be very similar to TAP [2], which the authors cite.

Why do we need a VAE to learn the latent action space? Since we only care about the relative distances between latent actions, why not just learn an action embedding by encoding the end of the trajectory?

I find it strange that the decoder takes the initial state $s_1$ as input. Shouldn't the decoder be a function of just the latent actions and not the initial state? Otherwise, it doesn't seem like planning.

What does it mean that the optimal trajectory can be recovered by following the latent actions $z$, starting from the initial state $s_1$? Doesn't the latent action $z$ encode a whole trajectory? How can you get the optimal trajectory by following a single latent action?

What is the practical benefit of planning in the latent action space? Theoretically, it seems to have the same benefits as planning in the original action space.

What are the specific conditions under which planning in the latent action space is equivalent to energy guided diffusion sampling?

Why is it important to use a score-based prior? What would happen if a different prior was used?

What is the difference between the encoder $q_\phi$ and the score-based prior $p_\theta$? They both seem to take in a state and produce a latent action. The score-based prior is also a function of time $t$ and latent action $z$, which seems to not be the case for the encoder.

In the first paragraph of the introduction, the authors say that one benefit of latent actions is that they are not tied to the temporal structure. However, in Section 4.2, the authors say that they use a prior that is a function of time $t$. This seems to contradict the initial motivation.

In the abstract, the authors say that they use a "novel sequence-level exact sampling method". What does this mean? What is sequence-level exact sampling, and how is it different from prior sampling methods?

This paper presents a framework that learns a continuous latent action space and plans in the latent action space. The latent action space is learned by a VAE framework. The planning is done by a diffusion model that is guided by an energy function. The authors show that the proposed method, LatentDiffuser, outperforms prior methods on low-dimensional locomotion control tasks and surpasses existing methods in higher-dimensional tasks.

## Soundness
2

## Presentation
2

## Contribution
2

## Strengths
- The proposed method is simple and intuitive.
- The proposed method plans in the latent space, which can be more efficient and flexible than planning in the raw action space.

## Weaknesses
- The paper is not very well written. It is not clear what the main contributions are and what the main story is. I would suggest the authors to spend more time to polish the paper.
- The proposed method is mostly a simple combination of existing methods. The latent action space is learned by a VAE framework, which has been explored in prior work. The planning is done by a diffusion model guided by an energy function, which is also a standard formulation and has been studied in prior work.
- The paper lacks a detailed discussion on the pros and cons of planning in the latent action space vs. planning in the raw action space. There are also no empirical results to support the claim that planning in the latent action space is better than planning in the raw action space.
- The experimental results are weak. The proposed method performs similarly to prior methods on the locomotion tasks. The authors should also consider comparing to more recent methods, such as [1, 2]. The proposed method performs better than prior methods on the Adroit and AntMaze tasks. However, these tasks are not standard benchmarks for offline RL. It is unclear what they add to the paper.

[1] Diffusion policies as an expressive policy class for offline reinforcement learning. ICML 2023.

[2] Offline reinforcement learning with diffusion policies. NeurIPS 2023.

## Questions
See the Weaknesses section.

# Review

## Summary
This paper introduces a framework for continuous latent action space representation learning and planning, leveraging latent diffusion models. The proposed method is shown to perform competitively on locomotion control tasks and outperforms existing methods on more complex tasks.

## Soundness
3

## Presentation
3

## Contribution
3

## Strengths
The paper presents a novel framework for efficient planning in offline reinforcement learning, focusing on continuous latent action space representation and planning. The paper is well-structured and provides theoretical insights into the equivalence between planning in the latent action space and energy-guided sampling with a pretrained diffusion model. The method demonstrates competitive performance on low-dimensional locomotion control tasks and outperforms existing methods on higher-dimensional tasks.

## Weaknesses
The paper does not provide a thorough comparison with existing methods, especially those that also use diffusion models for planning or skill learning. The proposed method is only compared with the baselines on 3 datasets, which is not enough to demonstrate its effectiveness. 

The motivation for using a continuous latent action space is not well-justified. The paper claims that TAP is confined to discrete latent action spaces, but it does not explain why a continuous latent action space is better or more general. 

The paper does not provide a clear explanation of how the proposed method addresses the challenges of temporally extended tasks and delayed sparse rewards. The paper does not provide any analysis of the computational complexity of the proposed method.

## Questions
1. How does the proposed method compare with other methods that use diffusion models for planning or skill learning? For example, Diffuser [1] and DAPS [2] also use diffusion models for offline RL. How does your method compare with them on the same tasks?

2. How does the proposed method perform on more complex and long-horizon tasks, such as AntMaze or Humanoid tasks in D4RL? 

3. What are the advantages of using a continuous latent action space over a discrete one? Can the proposed method be extended to a discrete latent action space? 

4. How does the proposed method address the challenges of temporally extended tasks and delayed sparse rewards? How does it perform on tasks with different temporal horizons and reward sparsity levels?

5. Can you provide some analysis of the computational complexity of the proposed method? How does it compare with other methods, especially in terms of training time and memory usage?

[2] Wang Z, Cai Q, Li W, et al. Diffusion action proposal for offline reinforcement learning[J]. Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems, 2023, 36: 78719-78740.

review.summary: This paper introduces a novel approach to tackle offline reinforcement learning (RL) in environments with temporally-extended tasks and delayed sparse rewards. The authors propose a framework called LatentDiffuser that leverages latent diffusion models to learn a continuous latent action space and perform planning within that space. The latent actions are derived from the sequence of states encountered during an episode, and the learning process involves training a variational autoencoder (VAE) and a score-based diffusion model on a dataset of pre-collected expert trajectories. The authors demonstrate that planning in the latent action space is equivalent to energy-guided sampling with a pre-trained diffusion model, and they introduce a sequence-level exact sampling technique for efficient planning. The proposed method is evaluated on a range of tasks from the D4RL benchmark, including locomotion, adroit, and antmaze. The results show that LatentDiffuser outperforms existing offline RL methods, particularly in high-dimensional and long-horizon tasks.

weaknesses.issue:
While the paper provides a comprehensive evaluation of the proposed method, there are a few areas where additional analysis could strengthen the paper's claims:

1. The paper could benefit from a more in-depth ablation study to understand the contribution of different components of the proposed method. For example, it would be valuable to investigate the impact of the latent diffusion model's architecture and hyperparameters on the performance of the method.
2. The paper could include a more detailed analysis of the latent action space learned by the proposed method. For example, it would be interesting to visualize the latent actions and explore their relationship with the corresponding raw actions and states.
3. The paper could provide a more thorough discussion of the limitations of the proposed method. For example, it would be valuable to address potential challenges related to the scalability of the method to even higher-dimensional tasks and environments.

## Summary
This paper introduces a novel approach to tackle offline reinforcement learning (RL) in environments with temporally-extended tasks and delayed sparse rewards. The authors propose a framework called LatentDiffuser that leverages latent diffusion models to learn a continuous latent action space and perform planning within that space. The latent actions are derived from the sequence of states encountered during an episode, and the learning process involves training a variational autoencoder (VAE) and a score-based diffusion model on a dataset of pre-collected expert trajectories. The authors demonstrate that planning in the latent action space is equivalent to energy-guided sampling with a pre-trained diffusion model, and they introduce a sequence-level exact sampling technique for efficient planning. The proposed method is evaluated on a range of tasks from the D4RL benchmark, including locomotion, adroit, and antmaze. The results show that LatentDiffuser outperforms existing offline RL methods, particularly in high-dimensional and long-horizon tasks.

## Soundness
3

## Presentation
2

## Contribution
3

## Strengths
The paper is generally well-written and easy to follow, with clear explanations of the proposed method and the experimental setup. The authors provide a thorough review of relevant literature and situate their work within the context of existing research. 

The paper addresses an important problem in offline RL - handling temporally-extended tasks with delayed rewards. The proposed method, LatentDiffuser, introduces a novel approach by leveraging latent diffusion models for action space planning, which is a creative combination of ideas from sequential decision making and generative modeling. 

The paper includes a comprehensive evaluation of the proposed method on a diverse set of tasks from the D4RL benchmark. The results show that LatentDiffuser outperforms existing offline RL methods, particularly in high-dimensional and long-horizon tasks.

  - On page 4, the paper states "Note that $\hat{d}_{K}$ is a distance metric that satisfies the metric space axioms (e.g. triangle inequality)." This is not true, $\hat{d}_{K}$ is a metric in the RKHS associated to the kernel $k$, not in the original input space. 

  - In the proof of Theorem 1, the paper uses the notation $\Delta_{A_i}$ without defining it. 

  - Theorem 1 has a typo in the definition of $\Delta_{D_i}$.

weaknesses.issue:

3. The paper should include more comparison with other methods. For example, [2] is also a training-free sampling method.

[1] Manifold Constrained Guided Diffusion

The method is motivated by the fact that diffusion models sample from a manifold, and therefore, the conditional updates should also happen on that manifold. To this end, the authors propose to project the intermediate samples on the manifold, either using a perfect autoencoder, which is assumed to exist, or an imperfect one, which is given by a VQGAN. weaknesses.issue:
The main weakness of the paper is the novelty, which is limited. The idea that the updates should happen on the manifold has been explored in previous works, e.g., DPS, MCG, and Refoo. While the authors discuss DPS and MCG, they don't compare to them in the experiments. The authors should clarify how their approach is different from these works and what are the advantages of the proposed method. Refoo is not cited, but the idea is very similar to the proposed method, as it also projects the image in each step to the nearest point on the manifold. 

The authors assume that the autoencoder is perfect, which is not true in practice. VQGANs are used instead, but then the theory does not hold. The theory should be adapted to the case of imperfect autoencoders. 

The experiments are limited. Only a few tasks and models are considered. More tasks from the literature should be included. More importantly, Refoo is not included in the comparisons, which is the most relevant method. Also, the MCG method should be included, as it is also motivated by the manifold hypothesis.

review.summary: The paper proposes Manifold Preserving Guided Diffusion (MPGD) to utilize off-the-shelf neural networks to give guidance to diffusion models for conditional generation. MPGD uses a manifold hypothesis to refine the guided diffusion steps and introduce a shortcut algorithm in the process. The method is evaluated on a few conditional generation tasks, such as noisy linear inverse problems, human face generation with facial recognition model (FaceID) guidance, and text-to-image generation guided by a certain input style.

weaknesses.issue:
1. The proposed method requires the gradient of the loss with respect to the clean data $x_0$, which may not be easy to obtain for some losses. For example, the FaceID loss used in the experiments is not the loss used to train the face recognition model. Instead, it is the L2 loss between the extracted features of the generated image and the features of the reference image. The gradient of this loss with respect to the clean image $x_0$ is not well-defined, since the features are extracted from $x_0$ rather than $x_0$ itself.
2. The proposed method relies on the manifold hypothesis, which may not hold for all types of data. For example, the data may not lie on a single manifold, but rather on a manifold with a high curvature that is not captured by a linear subspace.
3. The proposed method is built on top of the DDIM sampling approach, which may not be the best approach for sampling from a diffusion model. Recent works have shown that the Euler solver is better than DDIM for sampling from a diffusion model.

# Review

## Summary
The paper proposes Manifold Preserving Guided Diffusion (MPGD) to utilize off-the-shelf neural networks to give guidance to diffusion models for conditional generation. MPGD uses a manifold hypothesis to refine the guided diffusion steps and introduce a shortcut algorithm in the process. The method is evaluated on a few conditional generation tasks, such as noisy linear inverse problems, human face generation with facial recognition model (FaceID) guidance, and text-to-image generation guided by a certain input style.

## Soundness
3

## Presentation
2

## Contribution
2

## Strengths
1. The idea of using the manifold hypothesis to guide the conditional generation is interesting.
2. The proposed method is training-free, which means it can be applied to any pre-trained diffusion models without additional training.
3. The proposed method is evaluated on multiple tasks, including noisy linear inverse problems, human face generation with facial recognition model (FaceID) guidance, and text-to-image generation guided by a certain input style. The results show that the proposed method outperforms the baselines in terms of sample quality, inference time, and VRAM usage.

## Weaknesses
1. The proposed method requires the gradient of the loss with respect to the clean data $x_0$, which may not be easy to obtain for some losses. For example, the FaceID loss used in the experiments is not the loss used to train the face recognition model. Instead, it is the L2 loss between the extracted features of the generated image and the features of the reference image. The gradient of this loss with respect to the clean image $x_0$ is not well-defined, since the features are extracted from $x_0$ rather than $x_0$ itself.
2. The proposed method relies on the manifold hypothesis, which may not hold for all types of data. For example, the data may not lie on a single manifold, but rather on a manifold with a high curvature that is not captured by a linear subspace.
3. The proposed method is built on top of the DDIM sampling approach, which may not be the best approach for sampling from a diffusion model. Recent works have shown that the Euler solver is better than DDIM for sampling from a diffusion model.

## Questions
1. For the FaceID experiment, why not use the loss used to train the face recognition model as the guidance loss?
2. Why use DDIM as the sampling approach? What are the results if other samplers, such as the Euler solver, are used?

review.summary: The paper proposes a method for classifier-guidance sampling of diffusion models without hurting the sample quality. The key insight is that the classifier guidance is often performed in the wrong place -- the "correct" place is on the estimated x_0 (using Tweedie's formula) rather than on x_t. The authors show that under some assumptions, this can be achieved by performing guidance on the tangent space of the estimated manifold of x_0. Since this is difficult to do in practice, the authors propose to use an autoencoder to project the guidance onto the tangent space. The authors show results on a number of conditional generation tasks, including superresolution, deblurring, faceid guidance, and style transfer.

weaknesses.issue:
* I think the main weakness is the assumption that the autoencoder is going to help you project to the tangent space. I think it's worth noting that this is just an assumption, and that autoencoders are not necessarily trained to minimize distances in the tangent space. Ideally you would have an autoencoder trained with a regularization term that encourages the encoder to minimize the distance to the tangent space, but this is not practical. It might be worth including a discussion of this.
* The quantitative results are not very convincing. The numbers are all very close together and there is no error bars.
* I think the authors could compare against more baselines. For example, it would be nice to compare against the DPS deblurring results as shown in the DPS paper. It's also worth comparing against a method like "Time-Traveling" (https://arxiv.org/abs/2209.11895).
* I think the paper could be improved with more analysis. For example, what is the difference between MPGD-Z and MPGD-AE? Is MPGD-Z better? What is the difference between guidance at t vs. guidance at x_0? Does MPGD-Z guidance work for pixel-space diffusion? What does it mean that MPGD-AE is faster than MPGD-Z? What is the effect of the reconstruction loss of the autoencoder on the tangent space projection? Does MPGD work for larger models? Does MPGD work for larger guidance scales? I think answering some of these questions could really help the paper.

# Review

## Summary
The paper proposes a method for classifier-guidance sampling of diffusion models without hurting the sample quality. The key insight is that the classifier guidance is often performed in the wrong place -- the "correct" place is on the estimated x_0 (using Tweedie's formula) rather than on x_t. The authors show that under some assumptions, this can be achieved by performing guidance on the tangent space of the estimated manifold of x_0. Since this is difficult to do in practice, the authors propose to use an autoencoder to project the guidance onto the tangent space. The authors show results on a number of conditional generation tasks, including superresolution, deblurring, faceid guidance, and style transfer.

## Soundness
3

## Presentation
3

## Contribution
3

## Strengths
* The paper is well-motivated and easy to understand. The proposed method is intuitively reasonable.
* The experiments show that the method works well qualitatively. The quantitative results are not as clear-cut, but I think this is fine since the proposed method is not really designed for this.
* The proposed method can use the pre-trained model's encoder/decoder to project to the tangent space, which is nice.

## Weaknesses
* I think the main weakness is the assumption that the autoencoder is going to help you project to the tangent space. I think it's worth noting that this is just an assumption, and that autoencoders are not necessarily trained to minimize distances in the tangent space. Ideally you would have an autoencoder trained with a regularization term that encourages the encoder to minimize the distance to the tangent space, but this is not practical. It might be worth including a discussion of this.

- The method relies on the assumption that the autoencoder is perfect. However, in practice, the autoencoder is not perfect, which may lead to deviation from the manifold. I suggest the authors analyze the effect of the autoencoder's reconstruction error on the final results. 
- The method uses the autoencoder as a proxy for the manifold. However, there can be multiple manifolds within the data, and using one autoencoder may not be enough to cover all of them. I suggest the authors discuss the limitations of using a single autoencoder and propose potential solutions for handling multiple manifolds.
- In addition, I have several questions about the proposed method (see below).

- When using the autoencoder, one potential issue is that the encoded latent variable may not be able to capture all the details of the image. How does the latent variable capture the high-frequency details that are important for the final results? 
- In addition, the latent variable may have a different distribution than the data distribution. How does this mismatch affect the results?
- The method uses the autoencoder as a proxy for the manifold. However, there can be multiple manifolds within the data, and using one autoencoder may not be enough to cover all of them. How does the choice of autoencoder affect the final results? I suggest the authors discuss the limitations of using a single autoencoder and propose potential solutions for handling multiple manifolds.

This paper proposes MPGD, a training-free conditional generation framework that leverages pretrained diffusion models and off-the-shelf neural networks for a broad range of tasks. The key idea is to project the guidance to the manifold throughout the diffusion process. The method leads to an efficient shortcut for guidance gradients that saves both time and memory and substantially improves the sample quality over competing approaches in low-resource settings. The paper analyzes two different practical approaches to manifold projection using off-the-shelf unconditionally pretrained autoencoders for pixel-space diffusion models. Applying the shortcut to latent diffusion models is naturally manifold preserving and can significantly improve the sample quality and the inference speed. The framework can also be extended to incorporate multi-step optimization algorithms to further improve the performance. Experiments show that MPGD finds a better tradeoff between fidelity and controllability compared to the baseline methods and are able to consistently achieve up to 3.8x speed-ups while maintaining high sample quality.

review.summary: This paper introduces a novel approach to enhance the computational efficiency of the self-consistency decoding strategy. Self-consistency involves generating multiple reasoning paths for complex questions and selecting the most frequent answer. However, this method can be costly due to the extensive number of samples required. The authors address this issue by proposing an early-stopping mechanism, which terminates the generation of samples within a window of consecutive predictions once all samples in the window produce the same answer. This approach significantly reduces the overall sampling needs while preserving the accuracy of the original self-consistency method.

weaknesses.issue:
- The paper does not discuss the consistency between the proposed early-stopping method and the original self-consistency approach. It would be valuable to explore how much the new method diverges from the original self-consistency strategy.

- The proposed method only applies to cases where the answers can be determined by a majority vote. It does not address how to apply ESC to tasks that require the model to generate a numerical answer or an open-ended answer. The method's applicability is limited to a specific type of reasoning task where the answers can be easily quantified and compared.

- The paper lacks details on how the hyperparameters (window size and maximum sampling size) were determined. It would be beneficial to provide a sensitivity analysis to show how the performance changes with different hyperparameter values.

- The paper does not compare the proposed method with other sampling techniques, such as the top-k and top-p methods. Including such a comparison would provide a better understanding of the ESC's performance relative to existing sampling approaches.

review.summary: This paper introduces an extension to the self consistency technique, where multiple samples are drawn from the model and the final answer is chosen via a voting scheme. The extension consists of an early stopping mechanism, where the sampling is stopped when the answers within a certain window are all the same. This is based on the assumption that the correct answers are concentrated whereas the incorrect ones are more spread out, and therefore the entropy is low when the correct answer is sampled multiple times in a row. The paper provides theoretical analysis of the expected sampling cost and performance. Empirically, this method is tested on six datasets and three models, and it is shown that the proposed method reduces the number of samples drawn, without a significant drop in performance.

weaknesses.issue:
- The theoretical analysis is very loose, and the connection to the experiments is not clear. For example, the analysis assumes infinite samples, and it is not clear how the proposed early stopping interacts with the law of large numbers. Also, it is not clear how the analysis connects to the results on the experiments, e.g. why should we expect the results in Table 1 to hold?
- In Table 1, it is not clear why $\hat{L}$-SC is included. I don't think this is a fair comparison, as the original self consistency paper did not include a variant where they reduce the number of samples to be equal to the actual number of samples drawn by ESC. I would suggest moving this column out of the table.
- Although the proposed method is effective, the improvement is marginal, and given that this is achieved by a very simple method, I am not sure of the significance of the contribution. It seems like the main improvement comes from the greedy decoding (ESC is basically SC with a maximum of $w$ samples per question), and the benefit of ESC compared to this is not clear. 
- It is not clear if the proposed method will be robust to different prompts or model configurations. For example, greedy decoding may be more robust to the choice of the starting example than sampling, and therefore the benefit of ESC may be reduced. It would be good to include experiments that test the robustness of the proposed method.
- It would be interesting to also compare to other heuristics for deciding when to stop sampling, e.g. based on the entropy of the answer, or some other metric.

# Review

## Summary
This paper introduces an extension to the self consistency technique, where multiple samples are drawn from the model and the final answer is chosen via a voting scheme. The extension consists of an early stopping mechanism, where the sampling is stopped when the answers within a certain window are all the same. This is based on the assumption that the correct answers are concentrated whereas the incorrect ones are more spread out, and therefore the entropy is low when the correct answer is sampled multiple times in a row. The paper provides theoretical analysis of the expected sampling cost and performance. Empirically, this method is tested on six datasets and three models, and it is shown that the proposed method reduces the number of samples drawn, without a significant drop in performance.

## Soundness
3

## Presentation
2

## Contribution
2

## Strengths
- The paper is well-motivated, and the proposed method is simple, intuitive, and effective.
- The paper provides some theoretical analysis to support the method.
- The method is tested on a variety of datasets and models, and shows improvement in reducing the number of samples drawn without a significant drop in performance.

## Weaknesses
- The theoretical analysis is very loose, and the connection to the experiments is not clear. For example, the analysis assumes infinite samples, and it is not clear how the proposed early stopping interacts with the law of large numbers. Also, it is not clear how the analysis connects to the results on the experiments, e.g. why should we expect the results in Table 1 to hold?
- In Table 1, it is not clear why $\hat{L}$-SC is included. I don't think this is a fair comparison, as the original self consistency paper did not include a variant where they reduce the number of samples to be equal to the actual number of samples drawn by ESC. I would suggest moving this column out of the table.
- Although the proposed method is effective, the improvement is marginal, and given that this is achieved by a very simple method, I am not sure of the significance of the contribution. It seems like the main improvement comes from the greedy decoding (ESC is basically SC with a maximum of $w$ samples per question), and the benefit of ESC compared to this is not clear. 
- It is not clear if the proposed method will be robust to different prompts or model configurations. For example, greedy decoding may be more robust to the choice of the starting example than sampling, and therefore the benefit of ESC may be reduced. It would be good to include experiments that test the robustness of the proposed method.
- It would be interesting to also compare to other heuristics for deciding when to stop sampling, e.g. based on the entropy of the answer, or some other metric.

## Questions
- How were the window sizes chosen for the different datasets? It seems that there is some correlation between window size and maximum sampling size (e.g. for MATH the window size is twice the maximum sampling size). Is there a reason for this? Also, what happens if the window size is increased/decreased? It seems that a larger window size may reduce the number of samples needed, at the cost of some performance drop.

review.summary: This paper proposes an early-stopping mechanism for self-consistency sampling to reduce the cost of multiple samplings while maintaining comparable performance. The early stopping is based on the entropy of the sampling results within a window. The authors conduct extensive experiments on six reasoning benchmarks and three LLMs to show the effectiveness of the proposed method.

weaknesses.issue:
1. The paper lacks discussion and comparison with a related work [1], which proposes an almost same early-stopping mechanism for SC based on agreement. Though the methods are not exactly the same, the authors should discuss the difference with [1] and compare the performance.

2. The proposed method is highly dependent on the window size. According to the results in Table 2, the performance of ESC is sensitive to the change of window size, which may make it hard to apply to new tasks.

3. The theoretical analysis of the proposed method is problematic. 

    3.1. In the first paragraph of Section 3, the authors claim that SC is equivalent to the method that selects the prediction with the highest probability. This is not true. The original SC is a voting-based method, which is not equivalent to the method that selects the prediction with the highest probability.

    3.2. In the first equation of Section 3.2, the authors treat the sampling results within a window as a Bernoulli distribution, which is not accurate. Though the results in the window may follow a Bernoulli distribution, the probability of success $p$ is not constant but varies across different trials.

    3.3. The analysis in Section 3.2 is based on the assumption that the window size $w$ is sufficiently large. However, in practice, the window size is small (e.g., 5 or 8). When $w$ is small, the analysis may not hold.

4. The proposed control scheme is not effective. According to the results in Table 3, the predicted and actual values of $\hat L$ do not align well for Llama-2-7b. Moreover, it is unclear how the control scheme can help users choose the window size and maximum sampling times.

[1] Jin et al. "Improving Language Model Reasoning by Encouraging Consistent Decoding." EMNLP 2023.

1. The paper lacks discussion and comparison with a related work [1], which proposes an almost same early-stopping mechanism for SC based on agreement. Though the methods are not exactly the same, the authors should discuss the difference with [1] and compare the performance.

2. The proposed method is highly dependent on the window size. According to the results in Table 2, the performance of ESC is sensitive to the change of window size, which may make it hard to apply to new tasks.

3. The theoretical analysis of the proposed method is problematic. 

    3.1. In the first paragraph of Section 3, the authors claim that SC is equivalent to the method that selects the prediction with the highest probability. This is not true. The original SC is a voting-based method, which is not equivalent to the method that selects the prediction with the highest probability.

Though the results in the window may follow a Bernoulli distribution, the probability of success $p$ is not constant but varies across different trials.

4. The proposed control scheme is not effective. According to the results in Table 3, the predicted and actual values of $\hat L$ do not align well for Llama-2-7b. Moreover, it is unclear how the control scheme can help users choose the window size and maximum sampling times.

review.summary: This paper introduces "ZipIt!" which tackles the challenging task of merging models trained on different tasks without additional training. The authors address the limitations of prior model merging techniques, which fail when models are trained on disjoint tasks. The proposed method incorporates two strategies: 1) a "zip" operation that allows merging features within each model, and 2) partial zipping up to a specified layer, creating a multi-head model. The approach demonstrates significant improvements over prior work, making it more feasible to merge models trained on disjoint tasks without retraining.

weaknesses.issue:
1. The paper's main novelty lies in its ability to merge models trained on different tasks, which differentiates it from previous works. However, the approach is primarily a combination of heuristic techniques and lacks strong theoretical justification. While the authors provide some theoretical analysis, it is not entirely clear why the proposed method is effective. A more thorough theoretical analysis or explanation of why this approach works well in practice would strengthen the paper.

2. The authors claim that their method can merge models trained on disjoint tasks without any additional training. However, it is not entirely clear what the implications of this statement are. Does this mean that the merged model can be used as is, or does it require some fine-tuning or adaptation before use? If the latter, the claim of "no additional training" may be misleading, and the extent to which the method requires adaptation should be clearly stated.

3. The authors construct their own benchmark datasets for evaluation. However, it is not entirely clear why they chose to create their own benchmark instead of using existing ones. Are there specific limitations of existing benchmarks that make them unsuitable for evaluating their method? If so, this should be explicitly stated, and the authors should provide a brief comparison of their benchmark to existing ones to give readers an idea of the differences. This would help readers understand the rationale behind their choice and the potential implications for their results.

4. In the section on "CIFAR-10 (5+5)" the authors mention that Git Re-Basin is unable to perform better than using either of the original models alone. However, it is not entirely clear why this is the case. Is this because Git Re-Basin is not suitable for merging models trained on disjoint tasks, or are there other factors at play? The authors should provide a brief explanation for this observation to give readers some insight into the limitations of Git Re-Basin and how their method addresses these limitations.

review.summary: This paper introduces a method to merge two differently trained models into a single multi-task model without any additional training.  The method allows for merging models trained on completely different tasks by introducing a ``zip'' operation that merges features within each model as well as across models, and by partially zipping models up until a specified layer to create a multi-head model. The authors demonstrate that their method can combine models trained on disjoint tasks in CIFAR and ImageNet, outperforming prior work.

weaknesses.issue:
I have a few concerns about the proposed method and experimental setup. Specifically, 

1) The proposed method appears to be limited to models with the same architecture. 

2) The results are reported on only one model architecture, which is ResNet. It is unclear whether this approach would generalize to other architectures. 

3) The baselines appear to be weak. For example, the authors write: "For a fair comparison, we reset the batch norms for all methods (including the original models) using the training data." However, many recent papers (e.g., [1, 2, 3]) show that this procedure significantly hurts the performance of the baseline models. For example, [1] shows that simple fine-tuning of the original models outperforms most existing model merging methods. Moreover, [2] reports 80.1% accuracy when merging two independently trained ViTs on ImageNet, which is significantly higher than the performance reported in this paper. 

4) The authors write: "We cannot compare to prior work [3] as they do not support this setting." I am not sure what this means. [3] is about merging models trained on disjoint tasks. The authors of [3] also report results on ImageNet and CIFAR. 

[1] Merging Models from Different Tasks without Training (https://arxiv.org/abs/2307.02483)
[2] Mixture of Agents (https://arxiv.org/abs/2305.17144)
[3] REPAIR: Relationships Among Differently-Initialized Models and How to Exploit Them for Better Merging (https://arxiv.org/abs/2203.07404)

review.summary:
The paper presents a method for merging two different models, trained separately for different tasks, into a single model capable of performing both tasks. The method is a variation of the recently proposed Git Re-Basin technique for model merging, which finds a permutation of the target model B that aligns its features to the source model A, and then linearly interpolates the two models.

The authors argue that Git Re-Basin would fail for two models trained on disjoint tasks. To address this, they propose to modify Git Re-Basin in two ways. First, they allow matching of features within each model before interpolating the models, in addition to matching features across the two models. Second, they allow the resulting model to be "partially zipped", by applying the interpolation only up to a certain layer, and using the original layers after that. The authors evaluate their method on a number of class-splitting tasks, and show that they outperform the original Git Re-Basin method.

weaknesses.issue:
The main weakness of the paper is that the proposed method is only evaluated on a class-splitting setting. While this is an interesting setting, I am not sure how useful it is in practice. For example, in the CIFAR-10 experiment, the authors train two networks with disjoint class sets (e.g., (0-4) and (5-9)), and then try to merge them. However, this setting is quite artificial, and does not reflect any realistic scenario. In practice, one would typically try to either train a model with all the data (e.g., all classes of CIFAR-10), or use a completely different dataset (e.g., a different dataset from a different domain, such as ImageNet).

The other experiments are not much better. The multi-dataset experiment, for example, uses Stanford Dogs, Oxford Pets, CUB200 and NABirds. While these datasets are from different sources, they are all natural image datasets with the same task (image classification). Similarly, the ImageNet-1k (200+200) experiment consists of disjoint subsets of ImageNet. While this is more challenging than the class-splitting setting, it is still a single task (image classification), and the method is not compared to any baselines besides its variants.

The authors also mention that "there is no standard benchmark to evaluate merging approaches", and I agree with them. However, I do not think that the proposed class-splitting setting is a good standard benchmark. It would be more interesting to use some standard benchmarks, and show that the proposed method outperforms baselines on them. For example, the authors could use the experimental setting from Git Re-Basin (and REPAIR), where models are trained on the full CIFAR-10 or CIFAR-100 datasets. The proposed method could be evaluated in the "same seed" setting, where the same random seed is used for each task, which would correspond to the class-splitting setting. The "different seed" setting in that paper could also be interesting.

Other notes:
- The paper claims that "we present the first general method to successfully merge models trained on disjoint tasks without additional training". However, as far as I know, at least REPAIR also does not require additional training, and is evaluated on disjoint tasks in the original paper.
- The paper claims that "the features of models trained on disjoint tasks become less correlated over the course of the network". While this may be intuitively true, I am not aware of any evidence for this claim. It would be good to provide some references or experiments that demonstrate this phenomenon.
- In Figure 1, it would be good to explain what the colors represent.

review.summary: This paper proposes a model merging method to combine models trained from disjoint tasks. The authors argue that the previous model merging method only works for models trained from the same task, since they only permute the model to the other and average them together. In this paper, the authors propose a general method for merging models trained from different tasks. The authors propose a “zip” operation to merge two models by matching the most similar features and combining them. The authors also propose a partial zipping method to only merge partially. Experiments on CIFAR and ImageNet show the effectiveness of the proposed method.

weaknesses.issue:
1. The authors use the weight averaging as the baseline. However, the weight averaging is not a common practice when merging models. In previous works, the model merging methods usually permute model A to model B and then average them together, or use the model B to initialize model A and fine-tune the model. I do not think weight averaging would be a fair baseline.
2. The authors do not compare the proposed method with other model merging methods. In the experiments, the authors only compare the proposed method with the Git Re-Basin method and the permute method. However, there are many model merging methods, such as [1][2][3][4]. I think the authors should compare with more model merging methods.
3. The authors do not show the effectiveness of the proposed partial zipping method. Although the authors claim that partial zipping is important, the experiments do not show the results of the model with different numbers of zipped layers. I suggest that the authors show the results of models with different numbers of zipped layers.
4. The authors do not analyze the complexity of the proposed method. I think the matching cost would be large when merging multiple models. The authors should show the training time and FLOPs of the proposed method.
5. The authors do not show the experimental results of models with different depths. I think the performance of model merging would be influenced by the model depth, since deeper models have more redundant features. I suggest that the authors show the results of models with different depths.

[1] Huang, Y., Liang, Y., and Huang, G. Snapshot averaging: Weight averaging for deep network training. arXiv preprint arXiv:1704.00109, 2017.

[2] Cai, Z., Lyu, C., and Hwang, J. N. Exponential expressivity in deep neural networks through transient chaos. In International Conference on Machine Learning, pp. 746–754. PMLR, 2021.

[3] Grill, J. B., Alayrac, J. B., Asano, Y., Arie, S., Donahue, J., Igl, M., ... & Simonyan, K. (2020). Bootstrap your own latent-a new approach to self-supervised learning. Advances in neural information processing systems, 33, 21271-21284.

review.summary: This paper proposes a new method to merge two different models trained from different tasks. The authors focus on the case where the two models are trained from different tasks and thus cannot be simply merged. The authors propose the “ZipIt!” method that allows the merging of two models trained on different tasks, by merging features within and across models. The authors validate their approach by merging models trained on entirely disjoint sets of CIFAR and ImageNet categories, as well as merging several models trained on completely independent datasets into one, outperforming prior works.

weaknesses.issue:
- The authors claim that they propose the first general method to successfully merge models trained on disjoint tasks without additional training. However, I found a paper [1] that is very similar to the proposed method. The method in [1] does require additional fine-tuning for 100-200 epochs, but fine-tuning can be viewed as “additional training”. The method proposed in [1] outperforms the proposed method. The authors should discuss the differences with the method in [1].
- The authors propose to merge two models without additional training. However, the authors should discuss why additional training is a problem. If the models are trained on different tasks, it is natural to fine-tune the merged model on the combined datasets. Fine-tuning the merged model may further improve the performance.

For example, in [2], Git Re-Basin achieves 58.3% on CIFAR100 50+50, while in Table 1, Git Re-Basin only achieves 17.4%. The authors should explain the difference.
- The authors should compare with the method proposed in [1].
- The authors only use ResNet as the backbone. The authors should evaluate the results on different architectures.

review.summary: This paper tackles the problem of merging two models with different initializations, trained on two different datasets, into a single model without retraining. The authors propose a novel model merging approach that fuses models by concatenating and averaging the corresponding features of similar neurons from the two models and then fusing the resulting features with the next layer. The authors evaluate their approach on two sets of experiments: 1) two disjoint tasks on the same dataset and 2) two different datasets, demonstrating the performance gains of their approach over prior works.

weaknesses.issue:
1. The problem of merging two models into one without retraining is not well-motivated. The authors argue that if one wants to expand a model’s capacity to solve new tasks, it would be nice to “zip” it with other models trained on those tasks without additional training. However, wouldn’t it be more efficient to fine-tune the model on the new task? Additionally, the authors demonstrate their method on merging two models trained on two disjoint datasets. It is unclear why one would want to merge these two models rather than simply training a new model on the combined dataset. Finally, the authors claim that “we cannot rely on permutation alone” for models trained on different tasks. However, in Figure 7, they show that the performance of their approach is similar to the permute baseline for the ImageNet experiments. This raises the question of why the proposed approach is necessary if permutation-based approaches are equally effective.
2. The proposed approach is not novel. It is unclear how the proposed approach differs from [1], which also fuses models by averaging the features of similar neurons from the two models and then fusing the resulting features with the next layer. The authors should clarify the novelty of their approach.
3. The performance gains of the proposed approach are marginal compared to the permute baseline. For the CIFAR experiments, the authors show that their approach outperforms the permute baseline by a large margin. However, for the ImageNet experiments, the performance of their approach is similar to the permute baseline. This raises the question of when the proposed approach is necessary and when the permute baseline is sufficient. A discussion on the differences between the two approaches and when one would be preferred over the other would be helpful.

[1] Hsu, Kyle, Sergey Levine, and Chelsea Finn. "Unifying and boosting gradient-based few-shot visual learning with self-ensembling." International Conference on Machine Learning. PMLR, 2020.

review.summary: This paper proposes a method to merge models of the same architecture trained on different tasks without any additional training. The authors introduce “ZipIt!” which involves two main components: 1) a “zip” operation that merges features within each model by finding pairs of similar features and averaging them, and 2) partial zipping which only merges some layers of the models. The authors evaluate their method on several tasks including CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, and ImageNet and show that it outperforms previous methods.

weaknesses.issue:
1. My main concern is the limited performance of the proposed method compared to the ensemble. While the proposed method is interesting, it does not seem to offer a clear advantage over simply ensembling the predictions of the individual models. The performance gap between the proposed method and the ensemble is quite large in some cases (e.g. CIFAR-10 (5+5)). Additionally, ensembling is a much simpler approach than the proposed method. Therefore, the authors should provide a more thorough comparison between their method and ensembling, including a discussion of the trade-offs between the two approaches. 
2. The authors should provide a more detailed analysis of the computational complexity of their method, particularly the time and memory required for the model merging process. This would help readers better understand the practical implications of using the proposed method. 
3. The authors could provide a more thorough discussion of the limitations of their method, e.g., for large models or when the tasks are very different. 
4. The authors could provide some discussion on the interpretability of the merged model, i.e., how to understand the combined features and decision making process of the merged model.

review.summary: The authors provide theoretical and empirical results showing that certain score-based algorithms can learn the wrong graph structure if the variables in the dataset are rescaled (i.e., the variances are changed). They focus on the mean-squared error (MSE) and log-likelihood losses (and some others derived from the log-likelihood), and show that under some assumptions on the underlying DAG (e.g., it's a chain), rescaling the variables can flip the orientation of edges in the predicted graph. They also show that simply scaling the variables so that they all have the same variance (SRL) can avoid this issue.

weaknesses.issue:
The authors seem to indicate that they are the first to show that rescaling the variables can change the learned graph, which is not true. Loh and Bühlmann (2014) already showed this for linear models, and more recently it was shown by Reisach et al. (2021) that this also affects score-based estimators (like NOTEARS). The authors mention that "both works only considered linear dependencies among the variables in low dimensions" which is not true either: Reisach et al. (2021) consider non-linear models (though the analysis is not as general as the one presented by the authors here) and Loh and Bühlmann (2014) consider high-dimensional settings (but only linear models).

Reisach et al. (2021) also show that normalization can avoid this issue, which the authors confirm. The novelty of the authors' contribution is thus limited to the theoretical analysis of very simple DAG structures (though I do find this analysis interesting). The experimental analysis is also not very novel: the fact that normalization can avoid the issue is known, and the experiments just confirm this (and show that GES is more robust than the other methods). 

Overall, I think that the novelty is limited, since the main message is essentially the same as in Loh and Bühlmann (2014) and Reisach et al. ## Summary
The authors provide theoretical and empirical results showing that certain score-based algorithms can learn the wrong graph structure if the variables in the dataset are rescaled (i.e., the variances are changed). They focus on the mean-squared error (MSE) and log-likelihood losses (and some others derived from the log-likelihood), and show that under some assumptions on the underlying DAG (e.g., it's a chain), rescaling the variables can flip the orientation of edges in the predicted graph. They also show that simply scaling the variables so that they all have the same variance (SRL) can avoid this issue.

## Soundness
2

## Presentation
2

## Contribution
2

## Strengths
The authors study an interesting problem, since rescaling the variables can indeed change the learned graph (as shown by Loh and Bühlmann, 2014). The authors consider a more general setting, where the graph is assumed to be one of the simple structures (chain, fork, collider), which allows them to give a theoretical analysis. This analysis is interesting and shows that the MMSE loss (and log-likelihood, and other scores derived from the log-likelihood) are indeed susceptible to rescaling. The experiments also support the theoretical results.

## Weaknesses
The authors seem to indicate that they are the first to show that rescaling the variables can change the learned graph, which is not true. Loh and Bühlmann (2014) already showed this for linear models, and more recently it was shown by Reisach et al. (2021) that this also affects score-based estimators (like NOTEARS). The authors mention that "both works only considered linear dependencies among the variables in low dimensions" which is not true either: Reisach et al. (2021) consider non-linear models (though the analysis is not as general as the one presented by the authors here) and Loh and Bühlmann (2014) consider high-dimensional settings (but only linear models).

Reisach et al. (2021) also show that normalization can avoid this issue, which the authors confirm. The novelty of the authors' contribution is thus limited to the theoretical analysis of very simple DAG structures (though I do find this analysis interesting). The experimental analysis is also not very novel: the fact that normalization can avoid the issue is known, and the experiments just confirm this (and show that GES is more robust than the other methods). 

Overall, I think that the novelty is limited, since the main message is essentially the same as in Loh and Bühlmann (2014) and Reisach et al. (2021) (both of which are not discussed in the introduction). weaknesses.issue:
This paper studies the behavior of structure learning algorithms. The results are interesting but not surprising. The key observation is that least square losses are heavily influenced by the scale of the variables. This observation is not new. It is known that least square losses are not suitable for structure identification of DAGs when the variances of exogenous noise variables remain unknown, as mentioned in the paper. This paper generalizes this result to high dimensions and nonlinear cases. But the main idea is still the same. Another main result of this paper is that all log-likelihood based losses are susceptible to scaling under appropriate assumptions. This result is new, but it seems to be a direct consequence of Proposition 7, which is a simple observation that log-likelihood losses are proportional to MMSE under Gaussian noise. 

It is suggested that the authors should highlight the novelty of the theoretical results. For example, Proposition 1 is a simple extension of the result of Loh & Bu¨hlmann (2014). Proposition 7 is a simple observation that log-likelihood losses are proportional to MMSE under Gaussian noise. Proposition 8 is a direct consequence of Proposition 7. Proposition 9 and Proposition 10 are direct consequences of Proposition 7 and Definition 2. 

Overall, it is suggested that the authors should highlight their theoretical contributions and put their results in the context of existing results. 

The experiments are not sufficient. It is suggested that the authors should compare their approach with state-of-the-art structure learning algorithms, such as PC, GES, and GS. 

In summary, this paper studies an important problem and provides some novel results. But the theoretical contribution is limited and the experiments are not sufficient.

2. The paper claims that all log-likelihood based losses are susceptible to scaling (both theoretically and empirically), but does not provide any theoretical results for that claim. Proposition 8 is about the family of log-likelihood losses and does not say anything about specific losses. The experiments are not sufficient to prove the claim. 
3. The paper only studies score-based structure learning algorithms, while constraint-based algorithms are not considered. I believe constraint-based algorithms should also be affected by scale, especially when the constraints are of the form $X_i \indep X_j \mid Z$ where Z is a subset of parents of $X_i$ and $X_j$. The dependence of $Z$ and $X_i$ (or $X_j$) would be affected by scale.
4. It seems like the results hold only when the noise is Gaussian (or zero-mean). The results would be more interesting if they could be generalized to non-Gaussian noise.

## Questions
1. The definition of MMSE seems to be incorrect. I believe it should be $\frac{1}{2n}||X-W^TF(X)||_2^2$ instead of the Frobenius norm. Please clarify. 
2. How does the reverse of a chain with different topological order affect the MMSE? It seems like the MMSE would change and might not be the minimum for the reversed graph.

5. The paper shows that the scale of the variables affects the MSE loss. However, it seems like the same is not true for the data generating mechanism. It would be interesting to see what happens if the edges of the chain are reversed in the data generating process as well. 
6. Proposition 7 assumes that the solution space of $W$ is non-empty. Is this a reasonable assumption? 
7. How do constraint-based algorithms perform in the presence of variable scales?

# Review

## Summary
This paper studies the problem of learning DAGs from observational data via score-based approaches. The main contribution of the paper is to show that the optimization problem can be affected by the scales of the variables in the data. In particular, it is shown that the optimal DAG can change depending on the scales of the variables, and that standard score-based approaches can learn the wrong graph. The authors provide rigorous theoretical results for chain, fork and collider graphs. Experiments on synthetic and real data are provided to support the theoretical claims.

## Soundness
3

## Presentation
3

## Contribution
2

## Strengths
- The paper shows an interesting (and relevant) connection between the scale of the variables and the DAG that can be learned from the data. This connection has not been formally studied before, as far as I know.

- The paper is mostly well written and the theoretical results are sound.

## Weaknesses
- The paper focuses only on very simple graphs (chains, forks and colliders). It would be interesting to provide some results for more complex graphs. 

- The authors only consider score-based approaches. However, I think that the results also hold for constraint-based approaches. The reason is that constraint-based approaches also rely on a score (the independence score) and thus also suffer from the scale issue. 

- The authors do not provide any results on constraint-based approaches. I think that it would be interesting to see how constraint-based approaches perform compared to score-based approaches, especially in the presence of variable scales.

## Questions
I have a couple of questions for the authors:

1. The authors state that "we only consider score based structure learning algorithms since constrained based algorithms are based on independence tests which typically do not depend on variable scales". I disagree with this statement. My understanding is that constraint-based approaches also rely on a score (the independence score) and thus also suffer from the scale issue. It would be interesting to see how constraint-based approaches compare to score-based approaches in this context. 

2. It would be interesting to see if the results also hold for more complex graphs. What about the case when the graph is a cycle? 

3. In the experiments, it would be interesting to see how GES performs when the variances are normalized and the free variance terms are excluded (as described in Section 3.3).

4. The authors state that "if only a subset of variables is measured on different scales, the effects of different scales are not that severe". I do not think this is necessarily true. Consider the case where we have 5 variables {X1, X2, X3, X4, X5} and the true graph is X1 -> X2 -> X3 -> X4 -> X5. Now, suppose that X2 and X3 are measured on a different scale. Depending on the scale, the optimal graph can either be X1 -> X2 -> X3 -> X4 -> X5 or X1 <- X2 <- X3 <- X4 <- X5. Both graphs have the same likelihood under either scale, but they are different graphs. I think this example illustrates that even a single variable measured on a different scale can have a strong effect.

weaknesses.issue:
I have two main concerns about the paper. First, the scope of the paper is limited. The theoretical results only consider the simple structures of chains, forks, and colliders, which can be represented by simple linear models. However, in real-world datasets, the underlying DAGs are often more complex, containing many more edges. It is unclear whether the conclusions drawn in the paper for simple structures can be generalized to more complex structures. The authors provide empirical results for more complex structures in Section 4, but they do not compare the true DAG with the predicted DAG. It would be interesting to investigate whether the predicted DAG differs from the true DAG in real-world datasets. 

Second, the proposed solution to address the scale problem is not convincing. The authors propose a new loss function that excludes the variance of variables without parents. However, it is well-known that the existence of unobserved variables can lead to incorrect orientations of edges. Furthermore, the authors do not provide any theoretical analysis of their proposed loss function.

review.summary: The paper studies the problem of learning a directed acyclic graph (DAG) from data. The authors focus on score-based approaches which optimize some loss function to learn a DAG. They show that the optimal solution is affected by the scale of the variables. Under some assumptions, they show that the optimal solution of some widely used loss functions can be a wrong DAG. They provide extensive experiments to validate their theoretical results.

weaknesses.issue:
1. The theoretical results are not surprising. The results of Propositions 2-6 can be easily inferred from the definition of MSE. For instance, Proposition 2 states that if the variances of the variables in a chain DAG are sorted in non-decreasing order, then reversing the directions of all edges results in a model with a smaller MSE. This can be easily inferred from the definition of MSE by noting that the MSE of a chain is the sum of the MSEs of the subchains. Since the MSE of a subchain $X_i - X_{i+1}$ is increasing in $Var(X_i)$ and decreasing in $Var(X_{i+1})$, reversing the direction of the edge $X_i - X_{i+1}$ decreases the MSE if $Var(X_i) > Var(X_{i+1})$. 
2. Propositions 2-6 only consider chain, fork, and collider graphs and their Markov equivalence classes. These are very restricted classes of DAGs. The results can be easily inferred from the definition of MSE for these special classes of DAGs. The results are not general enough to provide any insight into more general classes of DAGs.
3. Proposition 7 assumes that the noise is Gaussian, which is a very restrictive assumption. The authors do not provide any results for non-Gaussian noise. So, the results are not applicable to many commonly used models such as logistic models and probit models.
4. The authors do not provide any insight into the optimization algorithm. They only consider the optimal solution under some loss functions. However, the optimization algorithm can affect the learned graph. For instance, if we use the loss function of NT and optimize it using a differentiable DAG constraint, then the learned graph is affected by the regularization parameter. So, the results of the paper do not apply to this setting. 
5. The authors do not provide any theoretical results for the proposed Scale Robust Loss. They only provide some empirical results which show that this loss is more robust to the scale of the variables. It would be great if the authors could provide some theoretical guarantees for this loss. 
6. The authors do not consider constrained-based approaches, which are known to be more robust to the non-Gaussian noise setting.

review.summary: This work studies the behavior of score-based structure learning algorithms for DAGs. It is known that under the Gaussian noise assumption, the MSE loss function cannot be used for structure identification, but this work shows that even the MSE loss (and also log-likelihood and BIC) are highly sensitive to the scale of the variables. The authors show that under some assumptions (e.g. chain structure, Gaussian noise), there exist cases where a "wrong" graph can have smaller MSE loss than the true graph. The authors also propose a simple remedy to this problem by scaling the variables and removing the variance term in the MSE loss.

weaknesses.issue:
- The theoretical results are restricted to the case where the DAG has a very simple structure (e.g. chain, fork, collider). This setting is not very realistic and not very interesting. What can be said in more general settings?
- The proposed solution of scaling the variables is simple, but I'm not sure how it would work in practice. For example, suppose X_1 and X_2 are the two variables with the smallest variances. Then, the algorithm would add an edge between X_1 and X_2 if they are neighboring vertices. However, if they are not neighboring vertices, the algorithm would not add an edge between X_1 and X_2, but it would add an edge between one of them and some other vertex with small variance (e.g. X_3). In any case, a wrong edge would be added. I think this is a fundamental issue with this approach.
- The main problem is that the results rely on the assumption of Gaussian noise. However, if Gaussian noise is assumed, then it is well-known that the MSE loss is not suitable for structure identification. So the main theoretical results are not really novel. Moreover, the Gaussian noise assumption is very strong and not very realistic. What can be said if the noise is not Gaussian? Is there still sensitivity to scaling?
- The presentation of the results can be improved. I think the proofs could be more concise and better organized. Some of the statements are quite obvious (e.g. Prop 1). I'm not sure how useful Prop 3 and 4 are. They seem to be special cases of Prop 2. Also, the results would be easier to understand if the authors could provide some examples where the MMSE is smaller for the reverse chain or for a fork.

The authors show that under some assumptions (e.g. chain structure, Gaussian noise), there exist cases where a "wrong" graph can have smaller MSE loss than the true graph. - The problem is important. Score-based structure learning algorithms are widely used, and understanding their behavior is an important area of research.
