review.summary: The paper proposes a large multimodal model that can understand referring expressions and ground them to regions or objects in an image. To achieve this, the authors first construct a dataset of text spans (noun phrases and referring expressions) linked to image regions using bounding boxes. Then they train a large multimodal model on this dataset together with existing image-text data. The model is trained to generate bounding boxes in response to text spans, and generate text spans in response to bounding boxes. The model is also trained to perform traditional next-token prediction on text as well as on location tokens corresponding to the bounding boxes. The authors evaluate the model on a wide range of tasks, including multimodal grounding, referring, perception-language and language understanding and generation tasks.

weaknesses.issue:
- The proposed approach is not novel. The authors propose to train a large multimodal model with a dataset of text spans linked to image regions using bounding boxes. However, this is the same as training an image-grounded LLM which is already studied in prior work [1, 2]. The authors should discuss these papers and compare to them.
- The paper claims that the model can “provide visual answers (i.e., bounding boxes)”. However, the evaluation does not include any tasks where the model is required to provide bounding box answers, only generation tasks are included. The authors should evaluate on tasks like SEED [3], ORD [4] and REACH [5].
- The authors claim that the model can “ground language to the visual world”. However, the referring expressions used in the paper are very simple and do not include spatial relations like “to the left of”, “above” etc. It is not clear how well the model will perform on more complex expressions. The authors should evaluate on datasets like SEED [3] and ORD [4].
- The performance of the model on the Flickr30K dataset is surprisingly low. According to Table 1 in the paper, Kosmos gets 65.2 CIDEr, and the proposed model gets 66.7. However, the original GPT-4 gets 80.3 CIDEr [6], and a simple CLIP+LLM model that just decodes class labels gets 67.1 CIDEr [7]. The authors should compare to these baselines.

[1] Li, Xiang, et al. "Align before fuse: Vision and language representation learning with momentum distillation." Advances in neural information processing systems 35 (2022): 9694-9705.

[2] Huang, Kaiyi, et al. "Learning to Prompt for Vision-Language Models." The Eleventh International Conference on Learning Representations.

[3] Zhu, Yuke, et al. "Seed: Semantics enhanced encoder-decoder framework for visual grounding." Proceedings of the IEEE/CVF conference on computer vision and pattern recognition. 2021.

[4] Yin, Dacheng, et al. "Optimal region discovery for visual grounding." Proceedings of the IEEE/CVF Conference on Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition. 2022.

2

## Presentation
2

## Strengths
The main contributions of the paper are:

1. The authors introduce a method for extracting grounded image-text pairs from existing datasets, which involves extracting text spans from captions and associating them with the corresponding regions in the image using off-the-shelf tools such as spaCy and GLIP. The resulting dataset, referred to as GrIT, contains approximately 90M images, 115M text spans, and 137M associated bounding boxes.

review.summary: This paper presents Kosmos-2, a multimodal large language model with grounding capability. To enable the grounding capability for MLLM, the authors collect a new dataset by linking the text spans in image captions to the corresponding image regions. The new data format represents the text spans and their bounding boxes as a markdown link, and the model is trained to predict the bounding box tokens corresponding to the given text span. Experimental results show that the proposed method can perform both grounding and referring tasks, while maintaining competitive performance on other vision-language and language tasks.

weaknesses.issue:
1. It seems that the authors train the model on both the old and new data formats, so it is unclear if the grounding capability can be added to the existing pretrained kosmos model.
2. The grounding capability of the proposed method is limited, as it can only output a single bounding box for each text span. For some complex text spans, the corresponding objects may be multiple objects or no object at all (if the description is not accurate), it is hard to define a unique mapping between the text span and the bounding box.
3. The results for language-only tasks are mixed. It is unclear why the grounding capability will harm the performance of some language tasks. The authors may need to provide more explanations and analysis.
4. For phrase grounding, the proposed method performs worse than the grounding-specific models without using any visual or language pretraining (e.g. VisualBert, MDETR, GLIP). It is unclear how much benefit the language and visual pretraining can bring.

review.summary: This work proposes to learn a language-informed visual concept representation for better disentangled and composable visual concepts. It proposes to use text anchors from VQA models for better disentanglement of the concepts. Experiments show that the proposed method can extract concept embeddings from a test image, which can be remixed to generate images with novel compositions of concepts.

For example, the results of changing only the color of the apple in Figure 3 (the first image). The results on single concept editing can better demonstrate the disentanglement of concepts. review.summary: This paper proposes a method to learn language-informed visual concepts from images, by distilling from a pretrained text-to-image model. After training, the learned concept encoders can disentangle different concepts, and allow recombination of concepts for new images. The authors use textual inversion to learn concept embeddings from an image, and use a VQA model to encourage disentanglement. The paper shows qualitative results of the concept embeddings being able to capture meaningful concepts, and shows how these can be combined. There are also some quantitative results on concept editing and a small human evaluation.

weaknesses.issue:
- It is unclear to me what is the main contribution of this paper. It seems like the main contribution is to learn a text embedding from an image using textual inversion, and use a pretrained VQA model to encourage disentanglement of the different concepts.

review.summary: The paper proposes a method for extracting language-informed visual concepts from images by distilling pre-trained vision-language models. The approach is similar to textual inversion. The difference is that instead of inverting a single token embedding for the entire image, the authors would like to predict multiple embeddings that correspond to different concepts that are present in the image. To achieve this, they prompt a VQA model to provide text descriptions of the concepts present in the image, and train a concept encoder to predict the concepts present in an image. The predicted concepts are then used with a frozen T2I model to generate new images. The authors show that this approach is able to extract concepts of different types (category, color, material, etc) from images, and that these concepts can be manipulated independently to generate new images with new compositions of concepts.

weaknesses.issue:
* The authors claim that their approach is novel. However, the work seems to be very similar to [1]. In [1], the authors use a similar approach to the one proposed in the paper to extract concepts from an image. The difference is that they use the extracted concepts to perform image editing instead of image generation. The authors should cite this paper and compare their results to [1].
* There are some missing details. For example, it is not clear how the concept encoders are trained. The authors mention that they use a CLIP ViT/L-14 model for image encoding, and then train K separate concept encoders on top of the features. However, it is not clear how this is done exactly. It would be helpful if the authors could provide more details on the architecture of the concept encoders and how they are trained.
* The results are limited to a single image. It would be nice to see if the results generalize to multiple images.
* The authors only consider 5 concepts (category, color, material, style, and season). It would be interesting to see if the approach generalizes to more concepts, and if the concepts can be easily disentangled when there are many concepts present in the image.

References:
[1] Chefer, Hila, et al. "Attend and Excite: Attention-Based Semantic Guidance for Text-to-Image Diffusion Models." arXiv preprint arXiv:2305.19327 (2023).

The key idea is to train a set of concept encoders to predict visual concept tokens to compose the image. The concept encoders are anchored to a set of text embeddings obtained from a pretrained VQA model (BLIP2) to encourage better disentanglement of different concept encoders. The authors demonstrate the usefulness of the learned concept encoders in recombining and extrapolating the concepts to new concepts.

weaknesses.issue:
- The problem of visual concept learning is not well-defined. What are the criteria for evaluating the visual concepts? It seems like the paper is focusing on visual concepts that can be described using attributes or adjectives. I would recommend clarifying the scope of the problem early on in the paper. 

- The paper does not provide any quantitative evaluation of the learned visual concepts. How good are the learned visual concepts? I would recommend quantitatively evaluating the quality of the learned concepts using some existing benchmarks such as CLEVRER (https://arxiv.org/abs/2003.03682). 

- The paper does not provide any comparisons to the methods that learn disentangled representations, such as beta-VAE (https://arxiv.org/abs/1703.04933) or infoGAN (https://arxiv.org/abs/1610.02502). It is not clear if the proposed approach provides any benefits over these methods.

review.summary: This paper proposed a method that aims to distill the visual concepts from pre-trained vision-language models. The method is trying to learn concept encoders to extract concept embeddings from a set of language-informed concept axes. The method is also able to generate new images with novel compositions of visual concepts. The experiments show that the proposed method can be applied to different concepts (e.g., color, category, etc.) and generalize to unseen concepts with lightweight finetuning.

weaknesses.issue:
- The paper's technical contribution is limited. The main contribution of this paper is to decompose concepts and represent them in the latent space. However, the way of representing concepts is not new. The proposed method uses CLIP to extract visual features and then uses an MLP to get the concept embeddings, which is similar to [1]. The paper should clearly state the technical differences between this paper and [1].
- The proposed method needs to train different encoders for different concepts. It is not clear how many encoders the method needs and how to design these encoders. Also, how does the number of encoders affect the performance?
- The experiment is not thorough. For the qualitative comparison, the authors only show results on one sample. More samples should be shown. Also, the comparison should include the results of each concept. For example, for the category and color, the authors should show more comparison results of changing category and changing color individually. The authors also should show more results of generalization to unseen concepts.
- The proposed method is not evaluated well. The quantitative results are only evaluated on one dataset with a limited number of samples. The evaluation dataset is also generated by the proposed method, which makes the results not convincing. Also, the evaluation focuses on the concept editing, which may not be suitable for evaluating the decomposition of concepts. A better way is to use the decomposed concepts to generate new images that contain only one concept. For example, changing the color of an image to red and generate a red object and a green object and then merging them together to form a new image that contains both red and green objects. If the image contains both red and green objects, it means the method can decompose concepts successfully.
- The paper does not have limitations and societal impact sections. The authors should add these two sections.

review.summary: The authors propose a method for learning visual concept representations in a disentangled way. This is achieved by optimizing concept embeddings using the objective of textual inversion. The authors use text anchors to encourage the embeddings to be disentangled. The authors use these concept embeddings to generate images with novel compositions of concepts.

weaknesses.issue:
1. The authors claim that their method learns disentangled representations. However, the evidence supporting this is very weak. The authors only show a few images of remixed concepts. It is not clear if the model actually learns disentangled representations. I suggest that the authors conduct an ablation study to test how changing one concept affects other concepts. For example, change the style of an image and measure the effect on the color embeddings. 
2. The authors say that they use Blip model predictions "only as anchors" to encourage concept disentanglement. However, there is no evidence in the paper to support that the model actually learns disentangled concepts. I suggest that the authors remove the anchors and show that the model is able to learn disentangled concepts on its own. 
3. The authors say that the method is different from [1] because [1] is focused on learning disentangled representations for video action recognition. However, I see [1] as a very relevant work since the goal of [1] is to learn disentangled representations for image generation. The goal of this paper is also image generation. I suggest that the authors compare against [1] and other disentanglement methods.
4. The authors claim that their method enables visual exploration. However, the results in Figure 8 of the appendix show that the model is not able to accurately change the style of the images. For example, the third row of the first column turns the image into a watercolor style, but the fourth row of the first column shows that the style was not changed. I suggest that the authors remove this claim from the paper unless they can show more convincing results. 
5. The method is not novel. Textual inversion is used to learn visual representations. The authors add an additional loss function to encourage disentanglement. However, this loss function is not well justified and there is no evidence to show that it results in disentangled representations. 

[1] Ranasinghe, Kanchana, et al. "Language-defined disentangled representations for video action recognition." Proceedings of the IEEE/CVF International Conference on Computer Vision. 2023.

The first objective is to reconstruct the input image through a pre-trained text-to-image model, using concept embeddings as input text.
The second objective is to align concept embeddings with text embeddings from a pre-trained VQA model, to encourage the disentanglement of different concept encoders.
After training, concept embeddings can be extracted from images and remixed to generate images with novel concept compositions.
The authors also show that with test-time finetuning, the model can generalize to unseen concepts.

## Soundness
3

## Presentation
3

## Contribution
3

## Strengths
- The paper is generally well-written and easy to follow.
- The proposed method is straightforward and simple, and is demonstrated to be effective.
- The authors conduct a variety of experiments to validate the proposed method, including both qualitative and quantitative comparisons with baselines and ablation studies.

## Weaknesses
- The evaluation in the paper is somewhat weak.
- The quantitative results are only based on the CLIP-alignment score and a small-scale human evaluation, and there is no qualitative user study to evaluate the image quality and the faithfulness to the instruction.
- The authors only conduct qualitative comparisons with two baselines, while there are many text-to-image generation methods that can achieve concept editing, such as ControlNet, DreamBooth, etc.
- There is no quantitative comparison with the baselines.
- The authors do not discuss the limitations and broader impacts of the proposed method in the paper.

## Questions
- The authors claim that the proposed method is able to capture the fine-grained visual nuances using continuous concept embeddings, but the provided qualitative results seem to only show results with discrete concept embeddings. How well does the model perform with continuous concept embeddings?
- How well does the model perform on natural images? All the provided results seem to be on synthetic images generated by DeepFloyd.
- The authors use the CLIP-alignment score to evaluate the method and conduct human evaluation with 20 people. However, it is not clear whether the CLIP-alignment score is a good metric to evaluate image editing, and 20 people seem to be a small-scale human evaluation. review.summary:
The paper proposes to learn language-informed visual concept representation by distilling large pre-trained vision-language models.
The method can encode the information pertinent to a set of language-informed concept axes and recompose the concepts to generate new images.

weaknesses.issue:
- The method can only be applied to the images with objects or concepts that can be described using a single word. It is hard to apply the method to more complex scenes.
- The method relies on the pre-trained VQA model to encourage the concept disentanglement. I am not sure if the VQA model can always give the disentangled answers. For example, what if the VQA model answers "green" for the question "what is the color of the object?" for an image of a green apple? In this case, the model may learn that the concept of "green apple" is represented by the concept "green" and "apple". How to ensure that the concept of "green apple" is represented by the concept "green" and the concept of "red apple" is represented by "red"?
- The method is only evaluated on the generated images. I am not sure if the method can work on real-world images.
- In the paper, the authors say that the method can generalize to unseen concepts with a lightweight test-time optimization procedure. I am not sure if the unseen concepts can be learned by simply finetuning the model on the new concept. The new concept may be very different from the existing concepts. For example, "airplane" and "car". "airplane" is a mode of transportation and "car" is a vehicle. They may be represented by very different embeddings.
- The method is compared with Null-text Inversion and InstructPix2Pix. I am not sure if these two methods are the most recent state-of-the-art methods. It would be great if the authors can compare the proposed method with more recent methods.

The main idea is to train a set of concept encoders such that their outputs, when provided to a text-to-image model, reconstruct the input image. weaknesses.issue:

The paper uses images generated from a text-to-image model and trains the concept encoders to reconstruct these images using the same text-to-image model. # Review

## Summary
The paper presents a method for learning a discrete set of concept encodings from images that can be learned via distilling a pretrained text-to-image diffusion model. The main idea is to train a set of concept encoders such that their outputs, when provided to a text-to-image model, reconstruct the input image. The paper shows that such concept encoders are disentangled and can be used for downstream tasks like image extrapolation and visual concept editing.

## Soundness
3

## Presentation
3

## Contribution
3

## Strengths
1. The idea of training concept encoders to reconstruct images via a text-to-image model is simple yet elegant. I have not seen this exact formulation in prior work and I think it has the potential to be useful for a number of downstream tasks.
2. The experiments are well-designed and the results are compelling. I particularly liked the visualizations and the qualitative comparisons. The paper also compares against the right baselines.
3. The paper is well-written and easy to follow.

## Weaknesses
1. My main concern is the choice of training data. The paper uses images generated from a text-to-image model and trains the concept encoders to reconstruct these images using the same text-to-image model. This is concerning because text-to-image models are not perfect and there is significant variation in the images they generate for a given text prompt. This essentially means that the concept encoders are being trained to reconstruct a noisy version of the concept and this may limit the model's ability to encode the concept precisely.
2. The experiments are limited in terms of the number of concepts used and the datasets considered. I think it would be interesting to see how the model performs on a larger set of concepts and on more diverse datasets.
3. I am not sure if I fully understand why the reconstructions look slightly off for some concepts, for example the "yellow" apples. Is this a limitation of the text-to-image model?

## Questions
1. The concept of "category" is a bit confusing to me. Is this supposed to be a generic concept like "object" or is it specific to a certain class of objects like "fruit"? 
2. How is the set of concepts chosen? Is there a particular reason to consider the given set of concepts?

# Review

## Summary
This paper proposed a simple and effective pruning method, termed Wanda, for large language models. It prunes weights with the smallest magnitudes multiplied by the corresponding input activations on a per-output basis. Wanda does not require retraining or weight update. Experiments on LLaMA and LLaMA-2 show that Wanda outperforms magnitude pruning and is competitive with SparseGPT.

## Soundness
3

## Presentation
3

## Contribution
3

## Strengths
- Pruning LLM is an important research problem. Wanda is simple and effective. It is good to see that such a simple method can be effective.
- Wanda is much faster than SparseGPT.
- Wanda outperforms magnitude pruning and is competitive with SparseGPT on LLaMA and LLaMA-2.
- The paper is well-written.

## Weaknesses
- The novelty is limited. As the authors discussed, Wanda can be seen as an approximation of SparseGPT by removing the off-diagonal elements in the Hessian. 
- The performance of Wanda is similar to SparseGPT. In particular, the results in Table 1 and Table 2 show that SparseGPT is better than Wanda in many cases.
- The authors claimed that Wanda does not induce any additional weight update. However, in Section 4, the authors discussed that Wanda can be naturally extended to structured N:M sparsity. Does the extension require weight update? In addition, I think that Wanda itself also implicitly involves weight update. For example, SparseGPT and Wanda use different pruning metrics. The weights pruned by Wanda are different from the weights pruned by SparseGPT. In other words, Wanda updated the weights.

## Questions
- Why is the comparison group defined as the weights connecting to the same output? Is it possible to use the same definition of comparison group as SparseGPT, i.e., the weights connecting to 128 consecutive input channels?
- Does the fine-tuning experiments use the same calibration data as pruning?
- Does Wanda outperform magnitude pruning and SparseGPT on other architectures, such as decoder-only models (e.g., BERT) and encoder-decoder models (e.g., T5)?

## Summary
This paper proposes a new pruning method called Wanda for Large Language Models (LLMs). The proposed method removes weights with the smallest magnitudes multiplied by the corresponding input activation norms, on a per-output basis. The key idea is to take into account the activation norms into account when pruning, which is a novel and effective approach. The paper evaluates Wanda on LLaMA and LLaMA-2 models and shows that it outperforms the baseline of magnitude pruning and is competitive with the state-of-the-art method SparseGPT.

## Soundness
3

## Presentation

## Contribution
3

## Strengths
1. The proposed method is novel and well-motivated, based on the key observation that activation norms should be taken into account when pruning weights in LLMs.
2. The paper presents a clear and concise description of the proposed method, which is easy to understand and implement.
3. The paper conducts thorough experiments on LLaMA and LLaMA-2 models and evaluates the performance on zero-shot tasks and language modeling. The results demonstrate that Wanda outperforms the baseline of magnitude pruning and is competitive with SparseGPT.

## Weaknesses
1. The paper lacks some ablation studies to further understand the proposed method. For example, it would be helpful to investigate the impact of the hyperparameter $\tau$ in the pruning metric, as well as the effect of the pruning configuration and the weight update strategy.
2. The paper does not provide any analysis of the learned sparse patterns by the proposed method. It would be interesting to visualize the sparse patterns and see how they differ from other pruning methods. This could provide some insights into why Wanda works well.

review.summary: The paper proposes a new pruning method for LLMs that does not require retraining or iterative weight updates. The method is based on the observation that the importance of a weight in a layer should be proportional to the magnitude of the corresponding weight multiplied by the norm of the input activation. This method is simple, efficient, and effective. It outperforms the baseline of magnitude-based pruning and is competitive with more complex pruning methods that involve weight updates.

weaknesses.issue:
- The novelty of the method is somewhat limited. The idea of using both the weight magnitude and the activation norm to estimate the importance of a weight has been explored in previous work, such as [1]. The main contribution of this paper is to apply this idea to LLMs and show its effectiveness.
- The method is not able to recover the performance of the dense model even after fine-tuning, especially for smaller models. For instance, the perplexity of the 7B dense model is 5.12, while the best perplexity of the 7B sparse model after fine-tuning is 5.98. This means there is still a significant gap between the dense and sparse models.
- The improvement over SparseGPT is marginal in some cases. For example, the perplexity of LLaMA-2 13B with 50% unstructured sparsity is 3.98 with SparseGPT and 3.98 with the proposed method. 

[1] Pruning neural networks at initialization: Why are we missing the mark?, ICLR 2021

## Presentation

## Strengths
- The method is simple and intuitive, and it is well-motivated by the observation of emergent large magnitude features in LLMs. 
- The pruning metric is very easy to compute and requires a single forward pass through the network. This is a significant advantage over methods that require iterative updates of the weights or the computation of the Hessian.
- The method outperforms the baseline of magnitude-based pruning and is competitive with the state-of-the-art pruning methods.

## Weaknesses
- The novelty of the method is somewhat limited. The idea of using both the weight magnitude and the activation norm to estimate the importance of a weight has been explored in previous work, such as [1]. The main contribution of this paper is to apply this idea to LLMs and show its effectiveness.
- The method is not able to recover the performance of the dense model even after fine-tuning, especially for smaller models. For instance, the perplexity of the 7B dense model is 5.12, while the best perplexity of the 7B sparse model after fine-tuning is 5.98. This means there is still a significant gap between the dense and sparse models.

review.summary: This paper introduces a simple method for pruning LLMs by combining the weight and activation. The method does not require re-training or weight update.

weaknesses.issue:
1. The novelty of this method is limited. The idea of combining weight and activation for pruning has been explored extensively in the past, including for LLMs. For example, [1] combines the weight and activation for pruning in CNNs. [2] and [3] combine the weight and activation for LLM pruning. Specifically, [3] uses the exact same idea as this paper: multiplying the weight and activation and pruning the weight with the smallest product. 

2. The paper overclaims its contribution. The paper claims that the method "outperforms the standard magnitude pruning by a large margin and also competes favorably with the prior best LLM pruning method". However, the performance of this method is almost always worse than SparseGPT. The only exception is at 4:8 sparsity on Llama2 7B. Since the performance is comparable, the only advantage of the proposed method is the speedup in computation, which is an implementation detail. I would recommend the authors to tune down the claims.

3. The method does not work well on smaller models. For example, in Table 1, the method is worse than SparseGPT on all Llama 7B settings. I am wondering if the method works well only on larger models.

[1] Accelerating Deep Network Training and Inference with Scalable Dot-Product Activation Pruning, NeurIPS 2020.

[2] MaPLe: Meromorphic Parity Learning for Language Model Pruning, ICLR 2023.

[3] LLM-Pruner: On the Structural Pruning of Large Language Models, NeurIPS 2023.

review.summary: This paper proposes a pruning method for LLMs, which does not need retraining or weight update. The idea is to use the product of the weight magnitude and the norm of input activations as the score to decide the importance of a weight. The proposed method is evaluated on LLaMA and LLaMA-2, outperforming the magnitude pruning baseline and being competitive to the SparseGPT method.

weaknesses.issue:
1. The novelty of the proposed method is limited. The proposed pruning metric is actually the absolute value of the element in the product of the weight matrix and the activation matrix. This is very similar to the element in the gradient, which is the absolute value of the derivative of the loss with respect to the weight. The derivative of the loss with respect to the weight is an estimate of the importance of the weight, which has been widely used for pruning neural networks. The similarity between the proposed method and the derivative of the loss makes the proposed method less novel.

2. The proposed method is not very effective. As shown in Table 1, the proposed method is not always better than SparseGPT. Moreover, for unstructured pruning, the accuracy of the pruned model is far away from the dense model. For structured 2:4 pruning, after finetuning, the accuracy of the pruned model is still about 1% worse than the dense model.

review.summary: The paper proposes a new method to prune LLMs. The method is based on multiplying the magnitude of the weights with the norm of the corresponding input activations. The weights are compared locally within each output of linear layers. The method does not require retraining, weight update or any kind of fine-tuning. The experiments show that the method outperforms the standard magnitude pruning by a large margin and also competes favorably with the prior best LLM pruning method (SparseGPT).

weaknesses.issue:
- The paper does not provide any results on how the pruning affects the inference speed of the model. The paper only provides the theoretical speedup based on the sparsity level. However, the actual inference speedup can be different due to various reasons.
- The proposed method is quite similar to the OBD (Optimal Brain Damage, 1991) method which is an old method for pruning neural networks. OBD also uses the first order Taylor approximation of the loss function and removes the weights with the smallest magnitude multiplied by the corresponding gradient. The main difference between Wanda and OBD is that OBD uses the gradient of the loss function while Wanda uses the norm of the corresponding input activations. However, the paper does not provide any discussion on this similarity and does not cite the OBD paper.

review.summary: The paper introduces a new method of training a multilingual vision-language model (VLM) efficiently. The method is based on the BLIP-2, which aligns a pretrained image encoder to a large language model (LLM). The authors start from a pre-trained English BLIP-2 model and re-align it with a multilingual LLM. The data for this re-alignment step is created by translating English data to 95 languages. The model is evaluated on image captioning and VQA tasks and compared to other multilingual VLMs.

weaknesses.issue:
The method is based on BLIP-2, which uses a query form to encode the image. A weakness of this architecture is that the query form has to be fed with text (the instruction), which is not ideal for multilingual. This is why the authors use LoRa to train the LLM in the re-alignment stage. However, this is not very efficient as only a few parameters are updated. It would have been better to use a more efficient architecture, like Flamingo, which encodes the image directly and does not need an extra query form.

The results are not really better than the other models, but they are comparable. However, the efficiency is better. The evaluation is extensive, but it would have been good with some human evaluation of the outputs. The data for the re-alignment step is created by translating the data to 95 languages. This data is then in English again, which means that the model has to learn to understand English. It would have been better with more multilingual data directly, which is one of the motivations for creating the model.

## Summary
The paper introduces a new method of training a multilingual vision-language model (VLM) efficiently. The method is based on the BLIP-2, which aligns a pretrained image encoder to a large language model (LLM). The authors start from a pre-trained English BLIP-2 model and re-align it with a multilingual LLM. The data for this re-alignment step is created by translating English data to 95 languages. The model is evaluated on image captioning and VQA tasks and compared to other multilingual VLMs.

## Soundness
3

## Presentation
2

3

## Strengths
The paper is well written and easy to follow. The paper has a clear motivation: to create a multilingual VLM efficiently. The method to achieve this is novel and makes sense: starting from an already existing monolingual VLM and re-aligning it to a multilingual LLM. The evaluation is extensive and the model is compared to other state-of-the-art models.

## Weaknesses
The method is based on BLIP-2, which uses a query form to encode the image. A weakness of this architecture is that the query form has to be fed with text (the instruction), which is not ideal for multilingual. This is why the authors use LoRa to train the LLM in the re-alignment stage. However, this is not very efficient as only a few parameters are updated. It would have been better to use a more efficient architecture, like Flamingo, which encodes the image directly and does not need an extra query form.

The results are not really better than the other models, but they are comparable. However, the efficiency is better. The evaluation is extensive, but it would have been good with some human evaluation of the outputs. The data for the re-alignment step is created by translating the data to 95 languages. This data is then in English again, which means that the model has to learn to understand English. It would have been better with more multilingual data directly, which is one of the motivations for creating the model.

## Questions
The paper is well written and I do not have many questions. What I do not understand is how you choose the multilingual LLM. You have chosen mT0-XL and BLOOMZ-7B. How do you choose between these two? How do you know if the model will work well in a low-resource language with mT0, but not with BLOOMZ? Or how do you know which one is better for English? This is not explained in the paper.

The experiments on image captioning and visual question answering show the effectiveness of the proposed method.

weaknesses.issue:
1. The novelty of the paper is limited. The proposed method is more like a multilingual version of BLIP-2, where a set of image-text pairs in multiple languages is used to adapt the model. The way of using the multilingual data is very simple, which is machine translation on the existing English datasets.
2. The paper does not discuss the difference between the proposed method and the simple baseline that trains a multilingual Q-Former and a multilingual LLM separately. The simple baseline can also achieve the multilingual vision-language model, and the performance of the simple baseline should be reported and compared.
3. The paper does not discuss the difference between the proposed method and the simple baseline that trains a multilingual Q-Former and freezes the Q-Former and trains a multilingual LLM separately. The simple baseline can also achieve the multilingual vision-language model, and the performance of the simple baseline should be reported and compared.
4. The proposed method is not efficient in terms of training data efficiency. The proposed method needs to use a large-scale English dataset and machine translation to achieve the multilingual model, while a simple baseline that trains a multilingual Q-Former and freezes the Q-Former and trains a multilingual LLM separately may be more efficient in terms of training data efficiency. 
5. The proposed method is not efficient in terms of training speed. The proposed method needs to train the Q-Former, while a simple baseline that trains a multilingual Q-Former and freezes the Q-Former and trains a multilingual LLM separately may be more efficient in terms of training speed. 
6. The performance of the proposed method is not good enough. The proposed method does not outperform a simple baseline that trains a multilingual Q-Former and freezes the Q-Former and trains a multilingual LLM separately.

The fine-tuning is performed by freezing both the image encoder and LLM and only updating the Q-former and the linear projection between them. The multilingual data is obtained by translating English data with NLLB. mBLIP is evaluated on several multilingual benchmarks and compared with several multilingual and English baselines.

weaknesses.issue:
- The results are behind previous work. While the proposed approach is simple and efficient, the results are behind previous work. For instance, PaLI-X (55B) outperforms mBLIP on XM3600 (Table 1) and PaLI and PaLI-X outperform mBLIP on xGQA (Table 2).
- There are several missing baselines. The paper does not compare with other efficient approaches such as BLIP-2 and InstructBLIP. In addition, there are other multilingual vision-LLMs such as M3P, UC2, and CCLM that are not included in the comparison. The authors argue that these models use a different architecture (encoder-only) but this is not a limitation of the proposed approach. On the contrary, the proposed approach also uses an encoder-only architecture and, therefore, cannot perform image captioning out-of-the-box. 
- The paper does not discuss the limitations of the proposed approach.

The main idea is to take a BLIP-2 model and align it to a multilingual LLM (e.g., mT5) by training a LORA on the LLM and finetuning a new query form on the translated version of the BLIP-2 training data. The authors show that the resulting model has competitive performance on multilingual captioning, VQA, and visual entailment tasks.

weaknesses.issue:
- The authors claim that the model was trained on "only" 2.5M images. However, this number is a bit deceiving since this data is obtained by translating the original data, which was used to train the original BLIP-2 model. So, in effect, the model was trained on the equivalent of 2.5M images in a different language. The real number of image-text pairs must be 5.1M (as stated in the footnote on page 4). The authors should clarify this in the abstract and/or in the introduction.
- One of the main motivations for the paper is that the resulting model is efficient and can be trained on a consumer-grade GPU. However, the results are not that good compared to other models. In Table 1, for example, PaLI-X (trained on much larger data) is better for English and the average of 35 languages. The results are better on some of the other tasks but overall I think the results are not that strong.
- The claim that the model supports 95 languages should be qualified. The authors did not test the model on 95 languages, but only on 36 (for captioning), 8 (for VQA), and 5 (for visual entailment). It is likely that the model does not work well for the remaining languages.
- The authors should consider adding a zero-shot experiment for the other models in Table 1. For example, PaLI-X was trained on much larger data and likely has better zero-shot performance. This would also help to understand the effect of the data distribution used by the model (see more comments below).

# Review

## Summary
This paper presents a multilingual extension to the BLIP-2 model. The main idea is to take a BLIP-2 model and align it to a multilingual LLM (e.g., mT5) by training a LORA on the LLM and finetuning a new query form on the translated version of the BLIP-2 training data. The authors show that the resulting model has competitive performance on multilingual captioning, VQA, and visual entailment tasks.

## Soundness
2

## Presentation
2

## Contribution
3

## Strengths
- The idea is simple and makes a lot of sense. I believe this will be a useful tool for the community in order to create a multilingual model without requiring a huge amount of data and compute.
- The paper is well written and easy to follow.
- The results are pretty good for low-resource languages.

## Weaknesses
- The authors claim that the model was trained on "only" 2.5M images. However, this number is a bit deceiving since this data is obtained by translating the original data, which was used to train the original BLIP-2 model. So, in effect, the model was trained on the equivalent of 2.5M images in a different language. The real number of image-text pairs must be 5.1M (as stated in the footnote on page 4). The authors should clarify this in the abstract and/or in the introduction.
- One of the main motivations for the paper is that the resulting model is efficient and can be trained on a consumer-grade GPU. However, the results are not that good compared to other models. In Table 1, for example, PaLI-X (trained on much larger data) is better for English and the average of 35 languages. The results are better on some of the other tasks but overall I think the results are not that strong.
- The claim that the model supports 95 languages should be qualified. The authors did not test the model on 95 languages, but only on 36 (for captioning), 8 (for VQA), and 5 (for visual entailment). It is likely that the model does not work well for the remaining languages.
- The authors should consider adding a zero-shot experiment for the other models in Table 1. For example, PaLI-X was trained on much larger data and likely has better zero-shot performance. This would also help to understand the effect of the data distribution used by the model (see more comments below).

## Questions
- I would suggest changing the name of the model. The name mBLIP sounds like an extension of BLIP, which is not the case since the underlying LLM is completely different. A more appropriate name would be something like CrossLingualBLIP or MultilingualBLIP.
- The authors should include the number of parameters and the compute used to train the model in Table 1. This would help to better understand the tradeoff between performance and compute/data.
- I would like to see a more detailed analysis on the effect of the data distribution used to train the model. How much does the model performance vary if you change the distribution of the languages? What is the impact of using a less diverse data distribution (e.g., only English, French, and Mandarin)? And what is the impact of using a more diverse data distribution (e.g., include all languages)? Also, how does this compare to the data distribution used by PaLI-X?
- In Table 1, the PaLI-X 0-shot row should be removed. I suggest adding a zero-shot row for the other models as well to better understand the effect of the training data. Also, I would suggest adding a row for the BLIP-2 model (or a subset of the training data).
- The authors should consider evaluating on more languages (e.g., all the languages from mC4) and adding a row for the model in Table 1. This would help to better understand the performance of the model on low-resource languages.

I think the authors should discuss the reason.

review.summary: The paper presents a method for multilingual VQA by re-aligning an English VLM to a multilingual LLM. The authors use machine translation to obtain data in multiple languages, and LoRA to parameter-efficiently fine-tune the VLM. They show strong results on multilingual VQA and captioning datasets.

weaknesses.issue:
- The main issue is novelty: the paper is essentially a straightforward application of the BLIP methodology to a multilingual setting, with the main difference being the use of LoRA. The results are interesting, but in my opinion not interesting enough for ICLR.
- There is a lot of focus on the amount of data used and the number of parameters, but I think this is a bit misnomer. weaknesses.issue:

The paper claims that the proposed method outperforms strong English-only vision-language models (VLMs) such as Llava 1.5. However, this is not an apples-to-apples comparison. In this case, Y is not monotonic w.r.t. Z but one can still identify the counterfactual Y_{Z=z}. 

- The paper does not seem to mention the key assumption that is required to identify the causal effect, which is that there are no unobserved confounders between X and Z, or equivalently, X and Z are independent in the presence of the common cause (see Pearl, 2009, Causal Inference Using the Algorithmic Markov Condition. # Review

## Summary
The authors use quantile regression to perform counterfactual inference. Their main claim is that, under some (strong) assumptions, counterfactuals can be identified using quantiles of the conditional CDF. They then propose a bi-level optimization scheme to estimate these quantiles.

## Soundness
2

## Presentation
3

## Contribution
2

## Strengths
The writing is clear and concise. The method is simple and intuitive, and it seems to perform well in practice.

## Weaknesses
The main weakness is that the identifiability result is stated very informally, and does not cover the most common case of interest: estimating the treatment effect. To be more specific: 

1. The assumption that $E \perp X, Z$ is very strong, as it is essentially a conditional independence assumption at the population level. This assumption is not needed in most of the literature, and even when it is needed, it is often placed as an assumption on a conditional model, not a SCM. For example, in the potential outcome framework, the usual assumption is that there is conditional independence between the error terms of treated and untreated units, not that the errors are independent at the population level. 

2. The assumption that $g$ is arbitrary is also quite strong. In particular, it would be good to discuss what happens when $g$ is a constant function. In that case, the SCM is essentially $Y = f(X, Z) + C$, which is not identifiable from an observational study (even in the potential outcome framework). 

3. It is also unclear why the main result (Theorem 1) is stated as a theorem, as it seems to be an immediate consequence of the definition of a SCM. It is fine to use this as motivation, but it is unclear why this is a theorem. 

4. It is also unclear why the main result does not cover treatment effect estimation, as discussed in the Questions section. 

5. It would be good to provide some more discussion on related works, particularly on identifiability results for counterfactuals. For example, [1] shows that under a conditional independence assumption on the errors, the causal effects are identifiable without a structural model. There are also several other works in this vein. 

[1] Learning Representations for Counterfactual Inference, Foster et al. 2021.

## Questions
My main question is why Theorem 1 does not cover treatment effect estimation. 

- First, the theorem assumes that $Z$ is a cause of $X$ (and hence, of $X_\text{treat}$ and $X_\text{control}$). However, in the potential outcome framework, treatment is often assumed to be exogenous. 

- Second, the SCM is assumed to be $Y = f(X, Z, E)$, but in the potential outcome framework, the causal effect of treatment is usually defined as the difference between the two conditional expectations, $f(X_\text{treat}, Z, E) - f(X_\text{control}, Z, E)$. Is the assumption that $E \perp X, Z$ strong enough to imply that $f(X_\text{treat}, Z, E) = f(X_\text{control}, Z, E)$, so that the treatment effect is always zero? If not, then it seems like Theorem 1 does not cover treatment effect estimation. 

It would be great if the authors could clarify this. 

Some typos:
- Definition 1: $X$ causes $Y$ should be $X$ causes $Y_{X=x'}$
- Definition 1: "the value of $E_Y$ is determined" is confusing phrasing, should be "the value of noise $E_Y$ is determined"
- Equation after line 137: $Y=y$ should be $Y=y'$

# Review

## Summary
This paper presents a real-time video enhancement framework designed to address practical video degradation issues, including low resolution, noise, blur, and compression artifacts. The framework employs a dual-branch structure. The first branch utilizes spatio-temporal features from a ConvNext-based encoder, while the second branch uses frame features from a mixer. The paper also introduces a recurrent framework where the prediction from the last frame is used to enhance the current frame, thereby improving temporal consistency. Additionally, the paper introduces two new datasets and provides extensive experimental evidence to support the proposed method.

## Soundness
3

## Presentation
3

## Contribution
2

## Strengths
1. The paper is easy to follow and clearly articulated. 
2. The proposed method achieves a good balance between visual quality and computational efficiency, making it suitable for practical applications such as video calls and live streaming. 
3. The paper introduces two new video enhancement datasets, which may benefit future research in this field. The proposed method demonstrates robustness in handling various types of video degradation.

## Weaknesses
1. The proposed method lacks novelty, as it is a straightforward combination of ConvNext and Mixer. 
2. The paper does not include an ablation study on the impact of the degradation on video quality. For example, it would be beneficial to explore how different types and levels of degradation affect the quality of the enhanced videos. This information would provide a deeper understanding of the method's robustness and its ability to handle various real-world scenarios.
3. The paper does not provide a comparison of the proposed method with state-of-the-art techniques on existing public datasets, such as the GoPro dataset for deblurring and the Vimeo-90k-T dataset for general video enhancement. Including such comparisons would strengthen the paper's claims and provide a more comprehensive evaluation of the proposed approach.

## Questions
1. The paper mentions that the second branch uses the Mixer on frame features. How does this branch handle the temporal dependencies in the video? Are there any additional mechanisms to address temporal consistency? 
2. How does the proposed method perform on existing public datasets, such as the GoPro dataset for deblurring and the Vimeo-90k-T dataset for general video enhancement? Including comparisons on these datasets would provide a more comprehensive evaluation of the proposed method.
3. What impact do the different types and levels of video degradation have on the quality of the enhanced videos? An ablation study on the degradation's effect would provide valuable insights into the method's robustness and its ability to handle various real-world scenarios.
4. The paper does not discuss the impact of the proposed method on the number of parameters. How does the model's size affect the performance and practical applicability of the method, especially in comparison to other state-of-the-art approaches?

review.summary: This paper introduces a new problem named selective FL (SFL), which aims to bridge the generic FL and personalized FL together. To solve the SFL problem, the authors propose a hot-pluggable FL framework, which first learns a global feature extractor and then learns multiple personalized plug-in modules. The authors also conduct experiments to show the effectiveness of the proposed method.

weaknesses.issue:
1. The new problem SFL is somewhat similar to the problem studied in [1], which also considers the test-time distribution shift of PMs. The authors should discuss the difference between the SFL and the problem in [1].
2. In Eq. (6), the authors aim to make the forward function of the client $i$ generate the same output of $f(\theta^{pfl}_{m},\xi_m)$ when meeting data $\xi_m\sim D_m$. However, how to guarantee the consistency of the two outputs? Why not directly use $\theta^{pfl}_{m}$ to train a $f(\xi_m)$?
3. The authors claim that PMs after PFL usually cannot achieve better performance on unseen data distributions than GM in GFL. However, in the experiments, the authors only show the results of PFL methods on local test datasets. I think the authors should also show the results of PFL methods on global test datasets.
4. In the experiments, the authors only consider the case where the number of clients is small. However, as the authors mention, one of the advantages of the proposed method is that it has good scalability. Thus, the authors should also evaluate the proposed method when the number of clients is large (e.g., 500).
5. The authors claim that the proposed method can protect the privacy of clients. However, to select a suitable plug-in module, the clients still need to download the auxiliary information of other clients. Thus, the proposed method cannot protect the privacy of clients from the inference attack. 
6. The authors only use FedAvg to train the feature extractor. However, as the authors mention, the feature extractor should be able to extract general features from all client datasets. Thus, more advanced GFL methods should be used to train the feature extractor.
7. The authors should compare the proposed method with the method in [1].

[1] Jiang, H., & Lin, Q. (2023). FedTHE: Test-Time Robust Personalized Federated Learning. arXiv preprint arXiv:2302.00962.

weaknesses.issue:
1. The proposed scenario seems to be a sub-case of federated learning with client selection. The difference is that the authors assume the test data is known at the client side and the client needs to generalize to this specific test dataset. In contrast, federated learning with client selection usually assumes that the server selects a subset of clients to train the global model, and the goal is to fit the whole training dataset. I would like to see a discussion on the relationship between the proposed scenario and federated learning with client selection.

The training of the global model is still based on existing methods. In particular, the authors consider a scenario where a client may encounter the test data from another client (different data distribution). To address this scenario, the authors propose a framework called hot-pluggable federated learning (HPFL) that consists of a globally trained feature extractor and a set of personalized models. During inference, the client downloads and uses the appropriate personalized model based on the test data. The authors claim that HPFL can achieve the high generalization performance on target data distribution and outperform the GFL and PFL baselines.

weaknesses.issue:
- The problem definition is unclear.
  - The problem is motivated by the scenario where a client may encounter the test data from another client (different data distribution). What does this mean? Does this scenario occur when the user of a weather app in the US travel to Japan? Then, why would the client in the US care about the temperature in Japan? Wouldn't it be more reasonable to assume that the user in Japan would use the model trained by clients in Japan?
  - In Table 1, the authors compare the performance of PFL against GFL on global test data and find that PFL performs poorly. Why should we compare PFL with GFL on the global test data? As PFL is trained to perform well on local test data, shouldn't we compare PFL with PFL on local test data? What is the purpose of this comparison?
- There is no theoretical guarantee of the proposed method.
- The experimental results are weak.
  - How do the authors partition the data for training and testing? The authors only mention that they use the Latent Dirichlet Sampling to partition the data for training. What about the test data? In the motivating example, the authors mention that a client in the US travels to Japan. How would the test data be partitioned in this case?
  - The authors assume that there are only 10 or 100 clients in the system. This is a very small number of clients compared to modern federated learning systems. The authors should conduct experiments with more clients.
  - The authors compare the proposed method with the FedAvg baseline. However, many advanced federated learning methods have been proposed in the literature. The authors should compare the proposed method with more baselines.
  - The authors use three neural network architectures in the experiment. However, two of them (MobileNet and simple-CNN) are not commonly used in the literature. The authors should use more common architectures such as VGG and WideResNet.
  - The authors report the average accuracy in the result tables. However, the authors should also report the variance of the accuracy to give a sense of how much the proposed method is sensitive to the initialization and data partitioning.
  - The authors should report the communication cost of the proposed method. How much data is transferred in the proposed method?

weaknesses.issue:
1. The proposed method is not well motivated. The authors claim that the proposed HPFL aims to let clients select and inference with suitable personalized models according to incoming test data. Besides, it is unclear how the auxiliary information $\mathcal{H}$ is obtained and whether it is related to the test data.

review.summary:
The paper deals with computed tomography and more specifically with the problem of reconstructing images when the reconstructed object contains high-density materials such as metal. In this situation, conventional reconstruction methods produce streak-like artifacts around the high-density regions. This is because the conventional reconstruction methods linearize the forward measurement model by applying the Beer-Lambert law. 

In this paper, the authors propose to directly reconstruct the signal from the raw nonlinear measurements. The authors show that gradient descent provably converges to the global optimum at a geometric rate. The authors also show that the number of measurements is near minimal. The authors also extend the results to the under-determined setting where the number of measurements is smaller than the dimension of the signal. This is achieved by enforcing prior structural information about the signal through constraints on the optimization variables. The authors also demonstrate the performance of the proposed method on synthetic and real 3D volumes.

weaknesses.issue:
- The paper does not report quantitative results, only qualitative results. This makes it hard to assess the quality of the reconstructions.
- The paper does not address the issue of noise in the measurements. The proposed method assumes noiseless measurements. However, in practice, the X-ray measurements are noisy.
- The proposed method is slower than the linear methods.
- The authors do not provide an analysis of the reconstruction time of the proposed method.

review.summary: This paper proposes a tomographic reconstruction method based on the non-linear forward model. Specifically, the authors consider the Beer-Lambert law as the non-linearity and show that gradient descent provably converges to the global optimum. The authors also extend the result to a compressive sensing setting with a convex regularizer. The authors conduct experiments on both synthetic and real data to verify the performance of the proposed method.

weaknesses.issue:
1. The non-linear reconstruction model considered in this paper is too simple. In practice, the Beer-Lambert law is only valid for a single attenuating material, which is not the case in real CT scans. For real CT scans, we have a mixture of multiple materials, and the Beer-Lambert law does not hold. The authors should consider a more general non-linear reconstruction model to better model the real CT scans.
2. The authors only consider the noiseless setting. In practice, the CT measurements always contain noise, and the authors should consider the noisy setting.
3. The authors only conduct experiments on a few phantoms and a single real dataset. More experimental results are needed to verify the performance of the proposed method.
4. The proposed method takes much longer than the traditional methods. The proposed method is an iterative optimization-based method, which takes much longer to converge than the traditional back-projection-based method. I think it would be better to include the computational time of the proposed method in the paper.
5. The proposed method is only applicable to a limited range of materials. In practice, the range of material that the CT system can detect is quite large, and it would be difficult to use the proposed method for the general setting.

The non-linearity is justified by the Beer-Lambert law and the observation that commercial CT scanners linearize the measurements by inverting the non-linearity. The paper would be stronger if there were a compelling application that is enabled by the non-linear model, and that would not be enabled by the linear model. The experimental results are a step in this direction, but it is not clear what is meant by "less metal artifacts". In any case, the paper could be improved by providing a stronger motivation for the problem.

## Questions
1. Is it the case that the linear model fails even in the presence of low-density materials? The paper mentions high-density materials such as metal, but I would expect that low-density materials (such as some types of tissue) would also cause problems for the linear model.

2. Is it possible to say anything about the ill-posedness of the problem? That is, if the linear model is ill-posed, is the non-linear model well-posed?

3. Theorems 1 and 2 state that GD converges to the global minimizer, though the rate of convergence is exponential only in the large sample rate regime. It would be interesting to know if the non-linear model has a unique minimizer, or if it has many minimizers so that GD is somehow finding a "lucky" one. Even if the non-linear model has a unique minimizer, there may be bad local minima that GD converges to.

4. Theorems 1 and 2 require that the number of measurements scales with the dimension of the signal. This seems very large, particularly for CT reconstruction where the image is of large dimension. Is this really necessary? Is this a limitation of the analysis?

5. Theorems 1 and 2 require a lower bound on the number of measurements. Is this necessary? In the linear case, 1 measurement suffices in some cases.

In fact, the proposed method is 5-10 times slower than the standard FBP method. Third, the authors did not consider other important aspects of CT reconstruction, such as the size of the reconstruction, the matrix size, and the sampling geometry. The size of the reconstruction is always large, and the matrix size is always huge. The sampling geometry is not uniform and it is always a fan-beam or 3D Cone Beam.

# Review

## Summary
This work considers the CT reconstruction problem. While the standard CT reconstruction approach is to use the (approximately) linear Radon transform as the forward model, this paper considers the use of the Beer-Lambert law, which is exact but leads to a non-convex reconstruction problem. The authors provide a theoretical analysis of an algorithm based on projected (sub)gradient descent, proving global convergence at a geometric rate, and provide some numerical experiments comparing the nonlinear approach to the standard linear approach.

## Soundness
3

## Presentation
3

## Contribution
3

## Strengths
The paper is clearly written and the theory is interesting and seems correct. The fact that this work provides a theoretical analysis for a nonlinear reconstruction algorithm is a nice contribution. The paper is also well-positioned in the context of the existing literature.

## Weaknesses
The main weaknesses of the paper are in the experiments, which are relatively limited and do not convincingly demonstrate the superiority of the proposed approach. The paper would be strengthened if the authors could provide more compelling experimental results.

## Questions
(1) The experimental results are not very convincing. First, the difference between the linear and nonlinear reconstructions in Figure 1 does not look very large (the linear reconstruction looks better). It is hard to believe that the artifacts shown in the linear reconstruction are due to the metal object - there appear to be similar artifacts in the same location in the nonlinear reconstruction. Also, the nonlinearity in the proposed model is due to the Beer-Lambert law, which should not produce these artifacts even in the presence of metal. The experimental results would be more convincing if the authors could show a case where the nonlinear reconstruction is clearly superior to the linear reconstruction.

(2) The authors should compare to additional baselines in the experiments. For example, there are many approaches for metal artifact reduction (see, e.g., "Removal of beam hardening effects in computed tomography" by V. N. S. Charalambous et al.). The authors should include at least one of these methods as a baseline. 

(3) The proposed approach is only for "beam hardening" CT - i.e., where the X-ray source is polychromatic. However, the majority of CT scanners are "beam-softening" (amorphous silicon flat panel detectors). The authors should discuss this.

(4) The authors should discuss the computational cost of their method. Reconstruction times should be reported for the experimental results, and the authors should discuss how their approach would scale to higher-dimensional problems.

The authors also extend the results to the case where the number of measurements $m$ is much smaller than the dimension of the signal $n$ by including a regularization term in the optimization problem.

The authors only provide two examples of reconstruction results, one with synthetic data and the other with real data. The proposed method uses a least-squares formulation, but it seems difficult to extend it to the case of Poisson measurement noise, which is common in CT imaging. This is because the least-squares loss is not robust to outliers, and Poisson noise often produces outliers in CT imaging. In practice, CT images often contain many outliers due to Poisson noise, and least-squares is not a good choice for this setting. In addition, the authors should discuss how to extend the proposed method to the case of Poisson noise.

## Summary
The paper proposes a tomographic reconstruction method that bypasses the linearization of the Beer-Lambert law by directly optimizing the measurements with the exponential nonlinearity in place. The authors show that the optimization problem can be solved by gradient descent, even in the case of highly absorbing materials, with good performance in terms of PSNR and in terms of metal artifacts.

## Soundness

## Strengths
The paper is well written, and the authors provide a good motivation for their work. The mathematical derivations are well explained, and the main contribution is clear.

## Weaknesses
The main weakness is the lack of a convincing argument for why the proposed method is useful. The authors propose to bypass the Beer-Lambert law and the linear Radon transform as a way to improve the reconstruction of highly-attenuating materials such as metal. However, they do not explain why a direct reconstruction through the Beer-Lambert transform is a better model of the measurement process. The paper does not discuss the presence of noise in the measurement process, and does not discuss the computational complexity of the proposed approach compared to current methods. In addition, the experimental results are not sufficient to demonstrate the superiority of the method in terms of metal artifacts.

## Questions
1. The authors claim that the reconstruction through the Beer-Lambert law is ill-conditioned in the vicinity of highly-attenuating materials. This claim should be supported by a detailed analysis of the problem, since this is the main motivation for the proposed method. The authors should discuss the effects of the nonlinearity and the noise on the reconstruction results, and explain why the linear approximation is not sufficient. This could include a comparison of the performance of the proposed method with a linearized model in terms of the Signal-to-Noise Ratio (SNR) or other relevant metrics.

2. The proposed method requires significantly more measurements (about 10 times) than the comparison method to achieve similar results. The authors should discuss the implications of this difference in terms of scan time and patient radiation exposure. They should also provide a more detailed analysis of the computational complexity of their method and compare it to existing approaches.

3. The paper does not address the issue of noise in the measurement process, which is a critical factor in CT reconstruction. The authors should discuss how the proposed method would perform in the presence of noise, and compare its performance to existing methods.

review.summary: The paper provides a theoretical analysis of the convergence of gradient descent for non-linear CT reconstruction. Specifically, the paper considers the situation when the Beer-Lambert law is applied, resulting in the non-linear measurement model $y_i = 1 - e^{-\langle a_i, x \rangle}$, where $a_i$ is a Gaussian random vector and $x$ is the unknown to be estimated. The paper shows that gradient descent converges to the global optimum at a geometric rate. The analysis is further extended to the regularized setting, where the number of measurements $m$ is much smaller than the dimension $n$ of the signal. Experiments are provided to illustrate the performance of the proposed method.

weaknesses.issue:
1. The practical relevance of the paper is unclear. The paper mentions that the Beer-Lambert law is used in CT scanners. However, it is not clear if the measurements exactly follow this model. Moreover, if the model does not exactly hold, the error between the model and the true measurements can be significant, and the theoretical results would not hold. 

2. The paper does not compare with prior work on non-linear inverse problems. The non-linear measurement model considered in the paper has been studied in the literature. See, e.g., the paper "Signal recovery in the presence of non-Gaussian measurement noise and non-linear measurement function" by A. Jung and A. Jung and A. Jung and R. Heckel. IEEE Trans. on Information Theory, 2021. The authors should discuss and compare with this prior work. 

3. The experimental results are not convincing. First, the paper only provides results on a single 2D image. It would be better to provide results on multiple images, so that one can see if the proposed method consistently provides better results. Second, the paper does not provide quantitative results in terms of PSNR or SSIM. It would be better to provide such results. It is also not clear if the proposed method actually removes the artifacts. Third, the paper does not provide an analysis of the reconstruction time of the proposed method. Since the proposed method is based on gradient descent, it may take a long time to reconstruct an image. Fourth, the paper does not compare with prior work on CT reconstruction. There are many methods in the literature for CT reconstruction. The authors should compare with some of them.

review.summary: This paper studies the optimization dynamics of deep neural networks. It focuses on the two key quantities, the restricted secant inequality and the error bound. The former measures the gradient alignment with the direction to the projection of the current point to the solution set, while the latter measures the gradient norm. Both quantities are important in understanding the behavior of stochastic first-order methods. The authors conduct a series of experiments on image classification, semantic segmentation and language modelling across different settings, such as batch sizes, architectures, optimizers and initializations. The experimental results show that these quantities remain stable and predictable throughout training, which further implies linear convergence. The authors also use the experimental results to prescribe learning rate schedules. This work provides novel insights into the properties of neural network loss functions, and opens the door to theoretical frameworks more relevant to practice.

weaknesses.issue:
1. The experimental results are not surprising. The secant inequality and the error bound are both related to the alignment of the gradient and the direction to the solution set. This means that the experimental results are expected to be positive and stable since the gradient is expected to be aligned with the direction to the solution set for most of the time. In addition, it is also expected that the experimental results become unstable when the algorithm is close to the solution.

2. The experiments are not comprehensive. The authors only consider image classification, semantic segmentation and language modeling. It is better to consider more applications, such as training autoencoders and GANs, especially the GANs with non-saturating losses.

3. The experiments are not sufficient. For example, the authors only consider the ResNet for image classification. It is better to include more model architectures, such as VGG and densenet.

review.summary: The paper studies the geometry of optimization paths in neural networks. Specifically, the authors consider the ratio of the restricted secant and the error bound. The latter are quantities that arise in optimization theory and are connected to the convergence of algorithms. In particular, the ratio is equal to the cosine similarity between the gradient and the direction of the iterate - optimum. The authors measure this quantity throughout training in different problems, datasets and architectures. They find that this quantity is mostly positive and stable. They also perform simple experiments on how this quantity behaves under different settings, such as different batch size, optimizers, and width/depth of the network.

weaknesses.issue:
I don't see a significant weakness in this work. The main concern I have is that the main observation, that the cosine similarity is mostly positive, is not that surprising. The authors do not really explain why this is the case. They perform various experiments, but I don't think that they quite capture the essence of the problem. I think that the paper could be much stronger if the authors could provide some explanation/insight as to why this happens. 

For example, one might expect that the cosine similarity should be close to one, since the direction of the gradient is mostly aligned with the direction of the optimum (which is also the case for the NTK, where the optimization path is aligned with the gradient direction). However, this is not the case in practice, since we see that the cosine similarity is not that high. On the other hand, one might expect it to be close to zero, since the direction of the gradient is mostly orthogonal to the direction of the optimum (as in the NTK in the kernel regime, where the optimization path is mostly orthogonal to the gradient direction). However, this is not the case in practice. Thus, it seems that there should be an explanation of why the cosine similarity is neither close to zero or one, but instead somewhat in between. 

I think that this is a very interesting question and a good understanding of it would shed light on the optimization dynamics of neural networks.
